Cam Schlittler laments what he couldn't do for Yankees with AL East hopes slipping away
PHOENIX — It was more than an hour since New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler threw a pitch Saturday evening, and he was still upset with himself.
He had another strong performance in the Yankees’ 5-3 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks, one that just about every starter in baseball would take − but they’re not Schlittler.
They’re not demanding perfection.
They’re not having one of the greatest seasons in baseball history.
So, when you give up just three hits and one earned run in six innings, it’s not good enough.
Not when you’re cruising to the Cy Young award with a 14-6 record and 1.94 ERA, yielding no more than one earned run in 22 of 32 starts, the best mark in Yankees history.
The 24-year-old has looked like Bob Gibson on the road, yielding an insane 1.16 ERA, the third-lowest in MLB history in a pitcher’s first 17 road starts. The only pitchers with a lower road ERA are Gibson in 1968 and Claude Hendrix in 1914.
Still, Schlittler didn’t care about any of that. All he knows is that the Yankees lost on Pavin Smith’s pinch-hit, two-run homer in the ninth inning, and he blamed himself.
He was livid that he couldn’t field a bunt in the fifth inning by Tim Tawa, and paid the price by giving up a two-run triple to Jordan Lawlar, with both runs unearned, coughing up a 2-1 lead. And after the Yankees took a 3-2 lead in the top of the sixth, he ran into control problems, throwing eight consecutive balls, and gave the lead right back, 3-3.
His night was over after six innings.
And, for the first time since Aug. 3, he gave up more than one run in a game, even though two of the runs were unearned.
“I mean, I wouldn’t say I really gave them a chance,’’ Schlittler said. “That one’s kind of on me, so I’ll take the blame for that. Made an error there, let up two runs.
“I mean, that’s baseball, but yeah, that one’s on me.’’
The loss all but mathematically eliminates the Yankees’ hopes of catching the Tampa Bay Rays for the AL East lead, even with a four-game series scheduled next week at Yankee Stadium. The Yankees (89-65) are five games back with just seven games remaining, with the Rays’ magic number dropping to 4.
“I mean, there’s still a chance,’’ Schlittler said, “but we got to play our (butts) off a little bit.’’
The reality is that the Yankees would have to sweep the Rays, needing to win all four games to win the tiebreaker, and still would need help.
“Mathematically, probably pretty tough,’’ Yankees outfielder Cody Bellinger said, “but you never know. … I mean, they’re playing tremendous baseball so it’s tough to climb up in the standings if they keep winning, right?
“So, mathematically, pretty tough, but got to keep on rolling.’’
The Yankees realize winning the AL East certainly has an inherent advantage with a first-round bye, which would give slugger Aaron Judge four more recovery days. But if they’re going to win their first World Series since 2009, they’re going to have to do it the hard way.
“The goal is obviously to win the division, rest your guys, get those extra off-days,’’ Bellinger said. “But ultimately, the World Series champion has come out of the wild card, so keep on fighting for the division, and we got to keep on rolling.’’
While the Yankees know it’s unrealistic to believe they can still win the division, they can at least start thinking about setting up their rotation for the postseason.
They can have Schlittler make one more start, perhaps even limit his innings, making sure he’s plenty rested, knowing that if they’re going to be playing deep into October, they’ll need to jump on his shoulders. He’ll be starting Game 1 of the postseason for them, being only the ninth pitcher in the 21st century to complete a season with a sub-2.00 ERA.
The Cy Young award belongs to him.
But he wants a World Series ring to go along with that hardware.
“The expectation is to make the playoffs,’’ Schlittler says, “and the expectation is to win a championship. That’s what I care about.’’
The Yankees know he’s special, putting on the greatest season by a Yankees pitcher since Ron Guidry in 1978, and know that when he takes the mound in October, he fully expects to win.
“He's a healthy combination between mature and immature,’’ Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. “I say that affectionately because look, he's really confident (in) what he does, which is a critical component to playing this game at this level. But he also doesn't take himself too seriously.
“I think he has a really good way of not being overwhelmed by really good results, which obviously he's had a lot of. Or even the moments and times where he struggled, he processes it real well, kind of matter-of-fact, and moves on.’’
The reality now is that the Yankees will be a wild-card team, and will host the Boston Red Sox in a best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium.
They also will have the greatest pitcher in the American League at their disposal.
“I’ll be ready,’’ Schlittler says.

Pavin Smith's pinch-hit, walk-off homer lifts D-backs over Yankees
(Photo credit: Arianna Grainey)
Pinch-hitter Pavin Smith hit a two-run walk-off homer with one out in the ninth and the Arizona Diamondbacks beat the New York Yankees 5-3 Saturday in Phoenix on a night the franchise celebrated the 25th anniversary of their 2001 World Series victory.
Ildemaro Vargas walked to lead off the ninth off Michael Fulmer (0-1), reaching base after he appealed the 3-2 pitch that originally was called a strike. After a strikeout, Smith hit a 389-foot homer to right center for the D-backs' 46th comeback win of the season
Heliot Ramos and Austin Wells hit bases-empty homers for the Yankees, who had won four of five and eight of 10. Wells and Jose Caballero had two hits apiece.
Nolan Arenado had two hits and Jordan Lawlar added a two-run triple for the D-backs, who had lost three in a row and five of six.
The Yankees (89-65), who have clinched a playoff berth, fell five games behind Tampa Bay (94-60) in the AL East and remained 5 1/2 games ahead of Boston (84-71) for the top AL wild card spot. The Yankees and Rays play a four-game series in Yankee Stadium beginning with a split doubleheader Tuesday.
The D-backs (81-74) gained a game on Philadelphia (85-70) for the third spot in the National League wild-card race but are still four games back with seven games to play.
Yankees starter and American League Cy Young candidate Cam Schlittler gave up three hits and three runs (one earned) in six innings, leaving when his pitch count reached 98. His season high is 106.
Schlittler struck out three and walked six while lowering his ERA to an American League-leading 1.94. He has given up one earned run or fewer in each of his last eight starts.
Arizona starter Brandon Pfaadt gave up four singles and one run in 4 1/3 innings, leaving after the Yankees loaded the bases on three singles in the fifth. Ben Rice hit a sacrifice fly off Justin Martinez to break a scoreless tie. Pfaadt struck out three and walked one.
The D-backs broke up Schlittler's no-hitter with a two-run fifth. Both runs scored after Schlittler's one-out fielding error.
Arenado had Arizona's first hit, a line single to left field with one out, before Tim Tawa pushed a bunt toward the mound. Schlittler could not field the ball cleanly and both runners were safe.
Lawlar lined a two-out triple to left-center on a 99 mph fastball for a 2-1 lead.
Ramos and Wells homered in the sixth to put the Yankees in front 3-2.
The D-backs tied it in the sixth when Ketel Marte and Gabriel Moreno drew four-pitch walks and Geraldo Perdomo beat out a two-strike bunt single to load the bases. Corbin Carroll hit a sacrifice fly before Schlittler struck out Arenado and Tawa with runners on second and third.
--Field Level Media

By DAVID BRANDT
PHOENIX (AP) — Pavin Smith hit a two-run homer in the ninth inning to lift the Arizona Diamondbacks over the New York Yankees 5-3 on Saturday night, giving the D-backs’ slim playoff hopes a boost.
Ildemaro Vargas started the ninth with a walk, winning an ABS challenge on a full-count pitch initially called a strike. After Jordan Lawlar struck out, Smith pinch hit and drove a cutter from Michael Fulmer (0-1) into the right-field seats.
Arizona pulled within four games of Philadelphia for the final NL wild card with seven games remaining, snapping a three-game losing streak on a night the franchise celebrated the 25th anniversary of its 2001 World Series win over the Yankees.
Juan Morillo (1-1) pitched 1 1/3 hitless innings. D-backs right-hander Brandon Pfaadt gave up one run on four hits and a walk over 4 1/3 innings, striking out three.
New York’s 11 walk-off losses are one behind San Francisco, which has the most in the major leagues.
New York ace Cam Schlittler gave up three runs — but only one earned — over six innings. The right-hander allowed three hits and three walks, striking out six and lowering his ERA to 1.94.
Schlitter’s 24 starts with one or no earned runs this year is one shy of the record in the live-ball era since 1920, set by Sandy Koufax in 1963, according to Major League Baseball.
The All-Star didn’t allow a hit until the fifth inning when Nolan Arenado lined a one-out single into left field. The right-hander then made a costly error on Tim Tawa’s sacrifice bunt attempt, dropping the ball as he tried to throw to first. Jordan Lawlar capitalized on the miscue with a two-out triple into the left-center field gap for a 2-1 lead.
Austin Wells and Heliot Ramos hit solo homers off Kevin Ginkel in the sixth to push the Yankees ahead 3-2.
Corbin Carroll hit a sacrifice fly in the bottom half but Schlittler limited damage by striking out Arenado and Tawa to end the threat.
Up next
1. Arizona RHP Corbin Burnes (0-0, 5.87 ERA) and Yankees RHP Will Warren (10-6, 3.89) start Sunday.

The New York Yankees suffered a tough loss on Saturday night, falling to the Arizona Diamondbacks 5-3 on Pavin Smith’s two-run walk-off home run in the ninth inning.
The loss came after the Yankees twice held a lead earlier in the game. New York broke through in the fifth inning when Austin Wells, Anthony Volpe and José Caballero opened the frame with consecutive singles to load the bases. Ben Rice followed with a sacrifice fly that brought home Wells and put the Yankees ahead 1-0.
Arizona answered in the bottom half of the inning, taking a 2-1 lead on Jordan Lawler’s two-run triple. Both runs were unearned against Yankees starter Cam Schlittler, who committed a fielding error on a sacrifice bunt during the inning.
New York responded quickly in the sixth. Heliot Ramos tied the game with a solo home run before Wells put the Yankees back in front with his 13th home run of the season. Both home runs came against Arizona reliever Kevin Ginkel.
Schlittler ran into trouble again in the bottom of the sixth after issuing two walks and allowing a single to load the bases with nobody out. Corbin Carroll tied the game with a sacrifice fly, but Schlittler struck out the next two batters to escape further damage.
Schlittler completed six innings, allowing three runs on three hits with three walks and six strikeouts over 98 pitches. Only one of the three runs was earned, and his season earned-run average dropped to 1.94.
Neither team scored again until the ninth, when Smith ended the game with his two-run homer off Michael Fulmer.
The Yankees will finish the series Sunday at 4:10 p.m. Will Warren will face Corbin Burnes.

Pavin Smith hit a walk-off two-run homer to secure the victory for Arizona.

Schlittler, the clear AL Cy Young favorite, was asked about the Yankees being five games back of the Rays.
New York Yankees Ace Cam Schlittler Makes Honest Statement After Loss to Diamondbacks
The New York Daily News’ Gary Phillips wrote on X:
Cam Schlittler on the #Yankees being 5 games behind the #Rays:
“We gotta go on a good run. It’s gonna be tough. I think we’ve had opportunities all season to put ourselves ahead, and we haven’t done a great job with it. So there’s still a chance, but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
Looking at the New York Yankees
The Yankees have the day off on Monday after they finish their series against the Diamondbacks on Sunday.
On Tuesday, New York is set to begin a four-game series against Tampa Bay, starting with a doubleheader.
At this point, the Yankees likely need to sweep the Rays to win the AL East. After the Rays series, the Yankees will host the Baltimore Orioles for three games, then the postseason will begin.
New York has already clinched a postseason spot, but it’s more likely the club will be a Wild Card team than a division winner.
With an 89-65 record, the Yankees are the first AL Wild Card team. They hold a 5 1/2-game lead over the Boston Red Sox, the second AL Wild Card team.
Most likely, the Yankees will host the Red Sox for a best-of-three Wild Card series. If the Yankees somehow win the AL East, they won’t have to play in the Wild Card round and will automatically earn a spot in the Division round.
The series finale of the three-game set between the Yankees and the Diamondbacks is scheduled to begin at 4:10 p.m. EDT on Sunday. Yankees fans can watch the game on the YES Network.

item.content:encoded:
One would figure that with Cam Schlittler going on Saturday night, this would be the game for the Yankees to win if they had any hope for a last-ditch AL East comeback, but something about Arizona wore down the likely Cy Young Award winner tonight. The Snakes were pesky, annoying, and other terms my editors won’t let me use while in the batter’s box tonight, finally breaking through on a Pavin Smith walk-off home run, to win it, 5-3.
Right off the top, I need to be grumpy about something. Nobody likes West Coast games and nobody likes the fact that every time the Yankees are on the West Coast, they play more night games than day games. This goes double for West Coast Yankee fans, because the beautiful thing about cheering for an East Coast team is they start playing when you get off work, or when you’re just finishing your Saturday morning coffee, the game takes three hours and you have the evening to yourself. That doesn’t happen on these trips.
Now, the Diamondbacks were celebrating the only World Series title in history, 25 years ago this season. I get it, you want to have a special event, the team isn’t very good so the end of the season starts to drag a little bit, you want a little spice. I even respect the cheek of waiting until the Yankees are in town. What I don’t respect is being completely incapable of running a functioning ceremony. The Yankees have Old Timer’s Day every year, they designate a special start time and at that time, the festivities have concluded and we can get down to the reason we’re all here, to watch a baseball game, which I don’t think is an unreasonable expectation at a baseball stadium with a baseball team in town.
The Diamondbacks started their pregame ceremonies at 4:30pm local time, with a scheduled 5:10pm first pitch. They absolutely blew past that in a way that, in my opinion, was both unprofessional and downright insulting. The four clocks I have ready access to in my apartment agreed: Brandon Pfaadt didn’t throw his first offering to Ben Rice until 5:42pm. This was an absolute joke of a start to the series’ second game. That all this happened in a city I’m predisposed to dislike already was…whatever the anti-cherry on top. I also firmly don’t like the existence of Phoenix as a city in general so I was always going to be ticked off watching this one.
I said in the gamethread that we had maybe begun to develop outsized expectations for Cam Schlittler. He’s been SO good, for long enough, that we needed to remember the other team all drives nice cars and lives in nice houses too. While Cam did get through 4.1 innings without allowing a hit, the Diamondbacks pushed a pair of runs across in the fifth. Nolan Arenado reached with a one-out single, before Tim Tawa attempted to give himself up with a sac bunt. Schlittler couldn’t corral what should have been an out though, an error that put two men on, and #9 hitter Jordan Lawlar made him pay:
Funny enough, because Schlittler was charged with that error, both of the runs were unearned, and he still hasn’t allowed more than a single earned run in eight starts now. The Yankees would tie the game the next inning, but all those extra pitches taxed his right arm, and I think had a major impact on what would happen in the sixth.
Speaking of tying the game, Heliot Ramos was brought to New York because of his opposite field power. He stunk in his first taste of East Coast baseball, but has looked much more representative in his last 20 games, and flexed that oppo pop within moments of Schlittler getting back in the dugout:
Corbin Carroll ran down a sinking Anthony Volpe liner for the second out, a very nice play that loomed larger when Austin Wells stepped to the plate:
Wells is getting hot at the right time, with three home runs in his last five games and he’s actually been a league average hitter since August 1! The nice thing about being a good defensive catcher is if you can just not embarrass yourself at the plate, you’re a major asset for your team.
The good vibes only lasted until Cam got back on the mound though. I think the error and the triple shook him up a little, and we’ve seen this happen before. Schlittler’s a high-energy guy, when that energy is less than positive I do think he gets a little in his own head and starts to overthrow. He walked the first two batters of the inning on eight total pitches, completely uncompetitive at-bats that are just so out of whack with what he’s done so far this season.
A soft Geraldo Perdomo bunt loaded the bases, and Cam did seem to lock in at that point. Corbin Carroll did bring in the third Snakes run of the game — and the only earned for Cam — but the ace got both Arenado and Tawa to whiff to end the threat. It was a weird one for Schlittler tonight, but 6.0 IP and one earned run is what the line reads.
The bullpen wasn’t exactly dynamite in Cam’s stead; the Diamondbacks have the third-lowest strikeout rate in baseball and their ability to grind out at-bats showed, even if the Yankees got through eight innings keeping the game tied at three. This was a long, miserable game, and wasn’t helped by the fact the Yankees couldn’t really find the nine-run spark that they showed on Friday.
If nothing else, I got to re-hate Michael Fulmer, and all those feelings from 2016 sprung forth anew. He walked the leadoff batter to open the ninth, and gave up the walk-off dinger to Pavin Smith:
The division race is functionally over with the Rays’ win earlier today, as they restored their five-game lead. Get yourself set for the Wild Card, lock up home-field advantage for that series, and don’t get yourselves hurt. The Yankes finish this series tomorrow with Will Warren on the hill. First pitch is supposedly at 4:10pm Eastern, but we’ll see.

ARIZONA – This one won’t hurt for the next 25 years, but it might sting for the next eight games.
On an evening when the D-backs turned back the clock to honor a World Series celebration that took place on this same diamond, it became the setting for another Yankees walk-off defeat – this one courtesy of Pavin Smith’s pinch-hit homer, sealing a 5-3 loss on Saturday at Chase Field.
Michael Fulmer took the loss, dropping the Yankees (89-65) five games behind the Rays (94-60) in the American League East with eight left to play, dimming their chances of avoiding a best-of-three AL Wild Card Series.
“We’ve got to go on a good run,” Cam Schlittler said. “It’s going to be tough. I think we’ve had opportunities all season to put ourselves ahead, and we haven’t done a great job of that. There’s still a chance, but we’ve got to play our [butts] off a little bit.”
Even with Saturday’s loss, the Yankees have won eight of 11, yet they have been unable to make up ground. The Rays walked off the Red Sox at Tropicana Field earlier Saturday, Tampa Bay’s seventh win in eight contests.
“They’re playing tremendous baseball. It’s tough to climb up in the standings if they keep winning,” Cody Bellinger said. “It’s mathematically pretty tough, but we’ve got to keep on rolling.”
The Yankees are scheduled to host the Rays for a four-game series that begins on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium.
“We sweep, and then it gets interesting,” manager Aaron Boone said. “But you can’t sweep before [Sunday’s] game.”
The sight of Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling draped in purple and gold as they hoisted the championship trophy atop the infield – just as they did that November evening in 2001 – offered a gut punch for Yankees fans who can clearly picture Luis Gonzalez’s hit sailing over a drawn-in infield.
For the next generation, another was delivered later. The frontrunner to win the American League Cy Young Award, Schlittler was dominant early, holding Arizona hitless until Nolan Arenado’s fifth-inning single.
Tim Tawa followed with a bunt back to the mound that Schlittler couldn’t handle cleanly, the ball falling out of his right hand. Four pitches later, Jordan Lawlar laced a two-run triple to the gap in left-center field, giving Arizona its first lead of the game.
Because of Schlittler’s error, both runs were unearned – though that offered no consolation to the right-hander.
“I’ll take the blame for that,” Schlittler said. “I made an error there and let up two runs. That’s baseball, but that one is on me.”
Heliot Ramos and Austin Wells homered in the sixth, but an uncharacteristic loss of command allowed the D-backs to tie the score.
Schlittler threw eight consecutive pitches out of the zone, then Geraldo Perdomo loaded the bases with a bunt single that third baseman Ryan McMahon fielded but couldn’t make a play on.
Corbin Carroll jumped on a high fastball to lift a sac fly off Schlittler, who struck out the next two batters to wrap his outing.
Schlittler finished the evening with a 1.94 ERA, allowing three runs (one earned) and three hits over six innings, walking three and striking out six.
“I felt like I made an adjustment after the second inning,” Schlittler said. “I was missing a couple arm-side. I made a good adjustment and lost the zone there [in the sixth]. Ultimately, it cost me.”
Though Schlittler was dissatisfied with his performance, Boone said he thought the right-hander “threw the ball great.”
“To get us through that sixth, it was a good job there,” Boone said.
Schlittler’s final start of the regular season is lined up to come during the series against Tampa Bay in the Bronx, carrying some statistical weight.
Schlittler has also allowed one earned run or none in 24 starts this season, joining Sandy Koufax (25 in 1963, 24 in 1966) and Bob Gibson (24 in 1968) as the only pitchers in the Live Ball Era with at least 24 starts of one earned run or none in a season (excluding openers).
Yet all the Yankees care about is making those four games mean something in the AL East race.
“Obviously, the goal is to win the division, rest your guys and get those off-days,” Bellinger said. “That’s always goal number one. Ultimately, World Series champions have come out of the Wild Card. We’ll keep on fighting.”

item.content:encoded:
Yankees at Diamondbacks. Cam Schlittler dominating in early innings
The Yankees broke through with the first run of the game in the top of the fifth inning, while the Diamondbacks are still looking for their first hit off Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler.
The Diamondbacks trail the Yankees, 1-0, after 4½ innings as play continued at Chase Field on Saturday, Sept. 19.
The Yankees loaded the bases on three singles in the fifth off right-hander Brandon Pfaadt, prompting manager Torey Lovullo to make an aggressive move to his bullpen. Right-hander Justin Martinez entered and recorded two fly-ball outs, the first of which, by Ben Rice, was deep enough to score the first run of the night.
The Diamondbacks are trying to keep their slim playoff hopes alive with a win. Meanwhile, the San Diego Padres, whom the Diamondbacks are hoping to catch, were losing to the Marlins at Petco Park.
The game started about a half-hour late after a lengthy pregame ceremony honoring the Diamondbacks’ 2001 World Series team.
With former radio voice Greg Schulte hosting the ceremony, the Diamondbacks introduced players, coaches and staff from the ‘01 team. Randy Johnson was the last one announced. While everyone else entered the field from beyond the right-field fence, Johnson came out of the home bullpen in left field, a call back to his relief appearance in Game 7 of the World Series.
One of the memorable moments of the pregame ceremony was when trumpeter Dr. Jesse McGuire, performing the national anthem as he did at the World Series in 2001, hit a sour note on his instrument. Then the trumpet gave out completely, and McGuire acted quickly by grabbing the microphone and singing the rest of the Star-Spangled Banner.
Afterward, he received a hug from Diamondbacks manager Torey Lovullo as the crowd cheered.
—Nick Piercoro and Jose M. Romero
With his team teetering on the brink of elimination, Lovullo’s job status is again a topic of discussion. Lovullo understands. For him, it’s nothing new.
“It seems to be a very important part of the conversation for a lot of people,” Lovullo said on Saturday, Sept. 19, a day after his team lost for the third consecutive day to drop five games out of a playoff spot with eight games remaining.
“For me, it’s real, I understand it, but it’s the realities of this game. You’ve got to win. That’s what it comes down to. Have we won enough? You know, I want to win every game that we play.”
Lovullo, in his 10th season as Diamondbacks manager, has worked as a “lame-duck” manager in four of the past six seasons. He seemed to reference that history, as well as the fact that he had to “fight for everything” during his playing career.
But he said that, for now, at least, he remains focused on doing what he can to help his players and coaches finish out the season.
“When it’s time to worry about it or think about it, whether that’s sooner than later, I will,” he said. “I’ve got to do my job. If I'm worried about different things that I can’t control, then I'm not doing my job for that group in there. I’m doing fine. I’m doing fine. Because I've lived in this space for a long time. I understand the playbook. I understand the realities of this game.”
Last year, Lovullo went into the final weekend of the year with similar questions surrounding him. He found out a day after the season ended that he would be coming back for another year.
The situation is believed to be similar to then: Lovullo has strong support from the baseball operations department and general manager Mike Hazen, but how he is viewed by ownership is less certain.
Lovullo has two postseason appearances — 2017 and 2023 — during his managerial tenure, but he also has presided over multiple late-season collapses. If this year's team continues to stumble, it would mark a third consecutive year the Diamondbacks fell short in September.
Hazen is working under the five-year extension he signed in September 2023. His deal runs through 2028.
The Diamondbacks entered Saturday, Sept. 19, facing long odds at a postseason berth. FanGraphs put their chances at claiming a wild-card spot at about 5%.
—Nick Piecoro
Justin Martinez leaves impression on manager
Members of the 2001 Diamondbacks World Series team milled about in front of the home dugout at Chase Field on Friday, Sept. 18, catching up, taking photos and conducting interviews.
Justin Martinez walked among them, asking each one he approached to sign a baseball. The Diamondbacks reliever later put the ball in a case he had with him in the team clubhouse.
Lovullo said Martinez seeking autographs of veterans is a throwback to a previous generation of players.
“I love it,” Lovullo said. “There was probably seven fistfights between those teammates, firstfights don’t happen anymore. It’s just a different level of camaraderie. But players care about the same thing, and that’s to win the world championship.
“So ‘J-Mart’ was probably just getting a feel for the common denominator based on what drove that team, and that’s a brotherhood that you can’t replace.”
Lovullo added that he's happy that the current team has players that are fans of baseball on that level.
“That he gets to touch their emotions makes it even better. That’s vintage J-Mart," Lovullo said.
— José M. Romero

Second year pitcher Cam Schlittler is the strong American League Cy Young candidate, but he may have a chance at another award. The New York Yankees ace continues to add to the great body of work and saw his ERA dropping below 2.00 in recent weeks. Schlittler has an outside chance at the AL MVP Award since he’s arguably the best player in the entire MLB right now.
ESPN’s Bradford Doolittle uses an advanced stats model, and it recently saw Schlittler moving up in the rankings via his AXE rating:
“Front-runner: Yordan Alvarez, Astros (146.9 AXE). Next: 2, Cam Schlittler, New York Yankees (143.0).
Schlitter has an uphill battle, but if I’d included pitchers in the MVP tables earlier, he would have been a fixture all season. Now he’s earning a little buzz both in articles speculating on awards consideration and the betting markets. I don’t think he’ll win, but for a 2026 starting pitching to get so prominently mentioned, that tells you all you need to know about how dynamic he has been.”
Doolittle confirmed that he expects Houston Astros slugger Alvarez to win the award since it’s extremely difficult for pitchers to take home MVP. However, he made sure to note that Schlittler making this race at all shows he’s having a historically great season for the contending Yankees roster.
How Cam Schlittler Can Win The MVP
Alvarez remains the strong favorite to win the AL MVP, but his Astros are still battling to make the playoffs. Houston is currently tied for first place in the American League West with the Texas Rangers both having 77-77 records.
Voters could punish Alvarez for team success if the Astros miss the playoffs and finish with a record under .500. Schlittler must hope for some luck of Houston failing and finishing his season strong with the Yankees having the second-best American League record.
An important start against the Tampa Bay Rays could see Schlittler having a “statement performance” if it helps the Yankees have a chance at the AL East title. Hitters getting the advantage in MVP voting requires Schlittler to finish perfectly to have a viable shot.
Current Betting Odds Hurt Cam Schlittler
Doolittle’s model is fully based off advanced stats, and fan discussions do little to help Schlittler’s case with baseball media. Current betting odds on various sports gambling sites see Schlittler still distantly behind Alvarez and Junior Caminero.
Bet MGM has the following odds for viable American League MVP candidates, as of September 19, 2026;
Alvarez: -2000
Caminero: +1100
Schlittler: +6000
Unfortunately for the Yankees and Schlittler, the odds show that it may be too late for him to make up ground in the narratives. Alvarez has been considered the favorite since he started putting up strong slugging numbers early in the season.
Schlittler should take pride in likely winning the Cy Young Award and even creating enough momentum to get any MVP consideration as a pitcher in 2026. The postseason will see Schlittler hoping to lead a rotation with Gerrit Cole and Max Fried to the World Series.

Last night was a good night for the Yankees, seeing the team put up five runs in the first paired with a good Gerrit Cole outing to cruise to a 9-2 win over the Diamondbacks. The club also picked up a game on the Rays as the AL East leaders dropped the opener of their series to the Red Sox. Tonight, the Yankees have two goals: get the win to stay in a hypothetically-competitive division race (all but necessary since Tampa Bay avenged the loss with a 2-1 win over Boston this afternoon), and build out a little more breathing room in the Cy Young race.
Dylan Cease had his worst start of the year on Friday for the Blue Jays, going just 2.2 innings and walking six. He and today's Yankee starter Cam Schlittler have had a heavyweight bout atop the Cy leaderboard all year, and while Cam's pulled away a bit in recent weeks, he can start to put the finishing touches on his case tonight. He hasn't allowed more than one earned run in a start since August 3rd (!!), making us all maybe expect a bit too much from the righty who can seemingly do no wrong. Schlittler has thrown 45 innings across those aforementioned seven starts, so he's not a five-and-fly guy, and his 1.00 ERA in that stretch is just…a farce.
Brandon Pfaadt is having the best season of his young career, with a 3.77 ERA and 4.06 FIP that are both significant steps forward after a pretty lost 2025. He doesn't strike many men out though, and a 45 percent ground ball rate means heavy sinking fastballs in the zone. There will be pitches to hit from Pfaadt; you just need to be able to elevate them.
Ben Rice had himself a fantastic game cleaning up last night and is bumped up to the leadoff spot tonight, with
Luis García Jr. getting the nod over Paul Goldschmidt at first base. Spencer Jones reportedly has a sore left foot, which means we get José Caballero in center, and I'm going to withhold comment on that decision for now.
It's an 8:10pm Eastern start but not a national broadcast, this one's on YES. The Diamondbacks will be celebrating their 2001 World Series championship throughout the evening, which seems kind of lame because you can't really "win" a championship when you didn't have an opponent.

The New York Yankees posted their starting lineup Saturday afternoon for the second game of a three-game set against the Arizona Diamondbacks, and Paul Goldschmidt was not in it.
New York is trying to take the series after a 9-2 win Friday night at Chase Field. Goldschmidt led off that game and finished with a hit, a walk and two runs scored.
The announced order put Ben Rice at designated hitter, Cody Bellinger in left field and Luis García Jr. at first base. Heliot Ramos started in right, George Lombard Jr. at shortstop, Austin Wells behind the plate, Anthony Volpe at second, Ryan McMahon at third and José Caballero in center. Cam Schlittler was listed as the starting pitcher.
Underdog MLB wrote: “Yankees 9/19 B. Rice DH C. Bellinger LF L. García Jr. 1B H. Ramos RF G. Lombard Jr. SS A. Wells C A. Volpe 2B R. McMahon 3B J. Caballero CF C. Schlittler SP.”
Goldschmidt, a seven-time All-Star, is in his second season with the Yankees after signing a one-year deal in February. He entered Saturday hitting .253 with 85 hits, 18 home runs, 50 RBIs, 44 runs and one stolen base in 102 games.
The 39-year-old first baseman spent his first eight big-league seasons in Arizona. He made six straight All-Star teams from 2013 through 2018 while wearing a Diamondbacks uniform.
After leaving Phoenix, Goldschmidt spent six years with the St. Louis Cardinals and won National League Most Valuable Player honors in 2022.
The Yankees sit second in the American League East at 89-64 through 153 games. They have gone 8-2 in their last 10 and trail the Tampa Bay Rays by four games.
Arizona is third in the National League West at 80-74 after 154 games and 4-6 over its last 10.
Manager Aaron Boone has mixed Goldschmidt’s playing time throughout the second half as younger options such as Rice have taken on larger roles. Goldschmidt started Friday after sitting in recent games.
The veteran remains a respected presence in the clubhouse. The Yankees nominated him for the 2026 MLBPAA Heart and Hustle Award earlier this season.
Goldschmidt signed a one-year, $4 million contract with New York this past offseason after hitting .274 with 10 homers and 45 RBIs in 146 games during his first Yankees season.
He has 390 career home runs and 1,282 RBIs across 16 major-league seasons. Career numbers also include a .286 batting average and seven All-Star selections.
Saturday’s game was scheduled for late afternoon local time. A New York win would give the Yankees the series with one game left.
The Diamondbacks have struggled to find consistent production at first base this year after Goldschmidt left the organization years earlier.
New York continues to chase a postseason berth in the final weeks of the regular season. Goldschmidt’s availability as a pinch-hitter or late-inning option remains part of the roster mix even when he does not start.
The lineup change was posted hours before first pitch and immediately circulated among fans tracking the club’s late-season decisions.

El rol regular de la campaña 2026 de la MLB está por llegar a su final para darle paso a la postemporada, sin dejar de lado las atractivas distinciones individuales para los mejores peloteros del año.
Entre ellos, emerge la figura de Cam Schlittler, el estelar brazo de los New York Yankees que ha pasado de ser un novato en 2025, a ser el máximo candidato para el Cy Young de la Liga Americana este año, acorde con la herramienta de seguimiento de premios MLB de ESPN.
Sin embargo, Cam ahora apunta a una distinción de mayor categoría y los números lo están respaldando seriamente para meterse en la conversación por el MVP de la Liga Americana, y la herramienta de medición es ni más ni menos que Clayton Kershaw, el último pitcher, sea en el joven o en el viejo circuito, que ha obtenido el galardón en las Ligas Mayores.
Las cifras que acercan a Cam Schlittler al histórico MVP que ganó Clayton Kershaw
Este 2026, Cam Schlittler ha puesto números muy cercanos a los que le valieron a Kershaw para ser reconocido como el MVP de la Liga Nacional en 2014. Desde el zurdo que hizo historia con Los Ángeles Dodgers, ningún otro lanzador de tiempo completo ha obtenido el reconocimiento.

Estas cifras están presentadas antes de la apertura de Cam Schlittler de este mismo sábado 19 de septiembre frente a los Arizona Diamondbacks, y considerando que a los Yankees aún les restan series ante los Tampa Bay Rays y los Baltimore Orioles, lo más probable es que el franela #31 de los ‘Mulos’ todavía tenga otra salida antes de la conclusión del rol regular de la campaña.
¿Puede realmente Schlittler ganar el MVP de la Liga Americana?
Aunque los números han sido espectaculares para el derecho de 25 años, la propia herramienta de seguimiento de premios MLB de ESPN indica que, en este momento, el favorito para ser reconocido como el jugador más valioso del joven circuito es, con buena diferencia, Yordan Álvarez.

As the 2026 MLB season comes to a close, the New York Yankees are playing to get the No. 1 seed in the American League. They are chasing their division rival Tampa Bay Rays and are four games behind them with nine games to play.
The Yankees will play a four-game midweek series with the Rays at Yankee Stadium starting this Tuesday, which will be a prime opportunity to gain some ground. For that series, it appears New York will get to throw their four best arms.
In a loaded starting rotation, there has been a clear No. 1 ace. That would be Cam Schlittler, the 25-year-old in his first full big league season. He has been so dominant that he is the runaway favorite to win the AL Cy Young Award.
MVP candidate
Sep 8, 2026; Bronx, New York, USA; New York Yankees pitcher Cam Schlittler (31) pitches against the Colorado Rockies during the fourth inning at Yankee Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
Schlittler has been elite to the point that he has been getting some MVP consideration from the media. The race in the AL this season is admittedly weak, with no one really having a season that stacks up to past winners.
That has opened the door for Schlittler, a pitcher, to perhaps get some first-place votes. The right-hander has made 31 starts this season, tossing 184 ⅔ innings. He is 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA, striking out 228 and walking 44.
This is one of the best pitching seasons the sport has seen in recent memory. On Saturday, MLB's official X account posted a comparison of him versus 2014 National League MVP Clayton Kershaw.
Kershaw and Schlittler
Kershaw was the last full-time pitcher to win the award, and did so by putting up statistics in the ballpark of Schlittler's. Kershaw only made 27 starts, but did throw more innings than Schlittler and did have a noticeably better ERA.
The Yankee ace probably will not win the award, but the fact that he is getting any consideration speaks to how good he has been. Schlittler was a seventh round draft pick by the team in 2022, so this run is honestly unprecedented.
The right-hander's next start will come Saturday at the Arizona Diamondbacks at 8:10 p.m. ET. This will be his second-to-last start of the regular season, as it has been reported he will likely go Thursday against the Rays in that crucial matchup.

Returning to the mound after missing an entire regular season due to an elbow injury is a daunting task for any pitcher. That context helps explain why Gerrit Cole endured a slow start to his 2026 campaign upon returning to the New York Yankees‘ rotation.
However, Cole’s recent surge on the bump has generated plenty of momentum within the organization. When asked whether the veteran righty would take the ball in the Wild Card round, manager Aaron Boone delivered a resolute answer: “I would expect Gerrit Cole to start, yes.”
Boone faces a compelling rotational dilemma, given the standout performances of his depth chart. Max Fried has anchored his share of gems, while breakout starter Cam Schlittler has delivered a dominant campaign, one that Boone firmly believes warrants American League Cy Young honors.
With Aaron Judge sidelined for the remainder of the regular season, the Yankees are relying heavily on their pitching depth to carry the load into October. That group could get another boost with Ryan Weathers tracking toward a postseason return.

Cole’s rollercoaster season
Cole’s season started with immediate frustration before he ever threw an official pitch. Lingering elbow concerns during Spring Training delayed his season debut, forcing him to miss the opening two months of the championship schedule and putting extra stress on the Yankees‘ starting rotation.
Dominant, double-digit strikeout performances—including a 10-strikeout shutout performance over 6.2 innings against Kansas City and multi-hit gems against Chicago and Atlanta—showed he remains one of the most electric arms in baseball.
A recurring issue throughout Cole’s 2026 campaign has been his home run rate. When Cole misses over the plate, opposing hitters have made him pay, elevating his HR/9 rate above his career averages and making several of his outings much more high-stress than his strikeout numbers would indicate.

Cam Schlittler has all but wrapped up the American League Cy Young Award.
The Pinstriped phenom is a -25000 favorite to become the seventh Yankee to win the honor at bet365 Sportsbook, and the biggest prediction markets, Kalshi and Polymarket, have him priced at 96 percent. There are no sure things in baseball nor in betting, but this one is pretty darn close.
While Schlittler will be making room for at least one award this winter, a debate has begun to spark up about whether the 25-year-old should also garner heavy consideration for another: AL MVP.
No pitcher has won the award in either league since Clayton Kershaw did so for the Dodgers in 2014.
Kershaw’s stat line that season was impeccable. He went 21-3, pitched to a 1.77 ERA and 0.86 WHIP, and racked up 239 strikeouts against just 31 walks in 198 1/3 innings. By season’s end, the future Hall-of-Famer had a WAR of 8.2.
Plenty has changed in baseball in the 12 years since Kershaw dominated the league, but Schlittler’s resume pops just as much. He leads the league in innings pitched, ERA, WHIP, and scoreless starts, and he’s second in strikeouts and quality starts. His 5.9 WAR at FanGraphs lags behind just Kansas City’s Bobby Witt Jr. (6.5) and Houston’s Yordan Alvarez (6.0) in the American League.
Alvarez, who was a Triple Crown threat for much of the year, is the -4000 favorite to be named AL MVP. Schlittler is currently priced at 50/1 at bet365 Sportsbook, making him the third-favorite, sandwiched between Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero and Witt Jr.
Caminero, who leads the American League with 41 home runs, is 14/1. Witt is 125/1.
Those odds suggest that the race is over. At -4000, Alvarez owns a 97.6-percent implied probability. Kalshi has it a shade lower at 89 percent. If that was the case, why did the Schlitter-for-MVP talks get so loud that his teammates shared their thoughts?
The answer is because the right-hander has a legitimate claim to the award. Not only by the numbers, but also by the literal meaning of the award. Who was the most valuable player to his team in 2026?
With Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, and Carlos Rodon all injured for large chunks of the season, Schlittler was the only Yankee starter that Aaron Boone was able to send out every five days. He took that responsibility head-on in his second season in the majors, delivering a 1.95 ERA, 0.90 WHIP, and 228 strikeouts in 184 2/3 innings so far.
Without that level of dominance, the Yankees could be scrapping for a wild-card spot; instead, they’re still in the hunt for the best record in the American League.
Schlittler has two starts remaining, likely against the Diamondbacks on Saturday and a potentially massive one versus the Rays on Thursday. If he is able to replicate what he did in his most recent outing against the Mets in those final two appearances, he’ll have plenty of voters thinking long and hard about whether he deserves this award.
At 50/1 odds this late in the season, it’s a chance worth taking.

item.content:encoded:
Friday was a bad day for the New York Yankees even though they opened their final road series of the regular season with a blowout win (NYY 9, ARI 2). Captain Aaron Judge is less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him more than three months. Judge's status for the rest of the season is up in the air.
"I don't have a timeline on him. I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires," manager Aaron Boone said (via MLB.com). "... The reality is, we've had to play a lot of the season this year without him. There's no replacing a player who is as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations. Those don't change now."
The Yankees are always cagey about Judge's injuries. They declined to reveal the severity of the calf strain or give a timetable for his return. Generally speaking, Grade 1 calf strains (the least severe) require 2-3 weeks on the injured list, though calves are very tricky and easy to reinjury. They must be allowed to heal fully, otherwise you risk a more severe injury.
For all intents and purposes, the Yankees are locked into the top wild-card spot. They're six games up in the loss column on the Boston Red Sox, who currently sit in the second wild card spot, plus the Yankees won the season series and have the tiebreaker, so it's really a seven-game lead. New York can clinch the top wild-card spot as soon as Sunday.
The AL East title remains mathematically possible, but it is a long shot. The Yankees are four games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the loss column with four head-to-head games remaining next week in the Bronx. The Rays only need to win one of those four games to clinch the season series and secure the tiebreaker, upping the difficulty for New York.
Just to lay it all out, here's what needs to happen for the Yankees to win the AL East, assuming they sweep those four games against the Rays and clinch the tiebreaker for themselves, which is a pretty big assumption:
- Rays go 6-3 or better: Rays win AL East
- Rays go 5-4: Yankees must go 9-0
- Rays go 4-5: Yankees must go 8-1
- Rays go 3-6: Yankees must go 7-2
- Rays go 2-7: Yankees must go 6-3
- Rays go 1-8: Yankees must go 5-4
- Rays go 0-9: Yankees must go 4-5
The Yankees have already clinched a postseason spot and winning the AL East was a long shot even with Judge. These last nine regular-season games are almost meaningless. If the AL East race gets interesting in a few days, the Yankees can shift gears, but the big picture takes priority this next week. Resting key relievers, lining up the rotation for the Wild Card Series, etc.
"Missing Judge, it hurts. We all know he's the best hitter in the game," Cody Bellinger said (via MLB.com). "For us in here, our mindset is, we're going to have to find a way. I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself. I'm fully confident that we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win, and beat anybody."
With the postseason less than two weeks away, Judge's calf injury creates a lot of questions for both him and the Yankees overall. Here are three questions for the man himself, and his team.
Three questions for Judge
1. Will he return for the postseason? This is really the only question, right? The Yankees are built around Judge being the best hitter in the world, and when he's not, the walls begin to cave in. New York had one of the lowest-scoring offenses in baseball when Judge was out with his rib injury. To paraphrase another New York baseball legend, Judge is the straw that stirs the drink.
Judge is eligible to come off the injured list next Sunday, the final day of the regular season. Roster-wise, he can return in time for the postseason. Health-wise, we have no idea. Calf strains are rarely 10-day absences, but that's what the Yankees have to hope is the case here. There's a very real chance the Yankees are without Judge for at least the Wild Card Series, and maybe longer.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason,” Aaron Judge said. “That’s definitely the plan.”
Said the calf strain involves the soleus muscle — which he said is more crucial to running and hitting — making it more difficult to play through.
2. Will he be himself at the plate? Judge did not go on a minor-league rehab assignment before returning from the rib injury and it showed. He went 4 for 23 (.174) with one walk and 13 strikeouts in his seven games back before the calf injury. His timing was not there at all. Judge's one homer came on a hanging breaking ball. Otherwise, pitchers threw fastballs by him consistently.
To put a number on it, Judge missed with 41% of his swings against fastballs in his seven games back, more than double the 19% league average. This is what it looks like when you miss with more than two out of every five swings against heaters:
It is not exactly a surprise a hitter who did not go on a rehab assignment after spending more than three months on the shelf looked out of sorts at the plate. Judge and the Yankees knew it would take him some time to get back up to speed at the plate, and they were willing to live with it. The goal was always to be ready for the postseason, not so much the regular season.
These last nine games aren't particularly important for the Yankees in the standings, but they were incredibly important to Judge. He needed at-bats to rediscover his timing at the plate, and get back to being the dominant hitter he's been throughout his career. The calf strain puts that on pause. Judge now has even fewer at-bats available to get back to being himself.
3. Will he be able to play the field? There is a scenario in which Judge plays through the calf strain as a full-time DH who doesn't run at 100% (or close to it). How the Yankees would align their defense in that scenario, I have no idea. Ben Rice is a full-time DH these days and also New York's best non-Judge hitter. Platoon-mates Luis Gárcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt are first basemen.
Unless the Yankees do something unexpected, like put Gárcia back at second base (where he was terrible defensively) or Rice back behind the plate (where he was also terrible defensively), slotting Judge in at DH means one of the team's most productive hitters will have to sit. This is something the Yankees will worry about when the time comes, and not a second sooner.
Three questions for the Yankees
1. Where will the righty pop come from? The Yankees have a very lefty-heavy lineup and Judge's righty heft provides important balance. Only the Cleveland Guardians have gotten fewer plate appearances from righties this season. Friday's lineup against Arizona Diamondbacks lefty Eduardo Rodriguez could be what the Yankees run out there against lefties in October:
- 1B Paul Goldschmidt, RHB
- LF Cody Bellinger, LHB
- RF Heliot Ramos, RHB
- DH Ben Rice, LHB
- 3B Amed Rosario, RHB
- CF Spencer Jones, LHB
- SS George Lombard Jr., RHB
- C Austin Wells, LHB
- 2B Anthony Volpe, RHB
Goldschmidt and Ramos are lefty mashers. Bellinger and Rice are very productive left-on-left hitters. Jones has performed well against lefties as a big leaguer, though his minor-league track record against southpaws isn't great. Rosario is having his worst season against lefties. The 7-8-9 spots are unlikely to make an impact offensively, regardless of the pitcher's handedness.
That lineup would look much more imposing with Judge in the No. 3 spot. Perhaps this is not such a big concern though? Since trade deadline day, the Yankees have the highest batting average (.289) and on-base percentage (.362) against lefties, and the third-highest slugging percentage (.456) despite Judge not playing much, and not being much of a factor when he did play.
In all likelihood the Yankees will host the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, and Boston has three quality lefty starters (Jake Bennett, Ranger Suárez, Payton Tolle) and a shutdown lefty relief tandem (Aroldis Chapman, Erik Miller). To beat the Red Sox, the Yankees will need their righty hitters to produce, and now the status of their best right-handed hitter is in question.
2. Will the pitching hold up? Despite not having Judge for more than three months, the Yankees have the American League's best run differential (+143) and second-best record (89-64). They can thank their pitching staff. New York has allowed only 3.68 runs per game this year, the fewest in baseball. Since trade deadline day, it's an incredible 3.37 runs allowed per game.
There are some cracks beginning to form, however. Gerrit Cole has surrendered eight home runs in his last three starts, including five on a four-seam fastball that is no longer the dominant pitch it was at his peak. Max Fried's velocity has been down a tick since returning from a bone bruise in his elbow late last month. That injury has sent him to the injured list twice this year.
Cam Schlittler, the AL Cy Young favorite, has thrown a career-high 184 ⅔ innings with two regular-season starts remaining, plus the postseason. Key late-inning relievers Paul Blackburn, David Bednar, and Brent Headrick have worked a lot -- A LOT -- this season and have all shown a slight dip in velocity in recent weeks, which perhaps is a sign the workload is catching up to them.
Without Judge (and sometimes even with him), the Yankees are a run prevention team. Their superpower is a suffocating pitching staff that is among the best in baseball at limiting hard contact, particularly in the air. With Judge absent, the pitching staff and the ability to prevent runs in general will be of paramount importance. No Judge reduces the margin of error considerably.
3. What about their other injured players? Judge is not the only injured Yankee. Center field Trent Grisham has not played since Sept. 4 due to a Grade 2 hamstring strain. On Friday, Boone said Grisham is pretty far into his running program, and he could make it back before the end of the regular season. That would give the outfield a lift should Judge miss extended time.
Second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. has not played since jamming his thumb sliding into second base on Sept. 8. Boone said Chisholm will come off the injured list when the Yankees return home next week. He's had a down year overall, but Chisholm was playing his best baseball of the season right before the injury. He's an important presence given his speed and defense in particular.
Left-hander Ryan Weathers is working his way back from a flexor strain. He last pitched Aug. 22. Weathers is throwing bullpen sessions, though Boone confirmed he won't return during the regular season. If/when Weathers does return, it will be as a reliever. He has bullpen experience and the Yankees could use middle relief help, but Weathers has to make it back first.
At minimum, Chisholm and Grisham would give the Yankees more options for their Judge-less lineup, even if they only platoon. It wouldn't be hard to find a role for Weathers, who had allowed no more than one run in six of his last seven starts before the injury. Bottom line though, the Yankees need Judge. Everything else is secondary to his return and effectiveness.

Gerrit Cole's two-game stretch against the San Diego Padres and the New York Mets raised concerns. With the postseason weeks away for the New York Yankees, Cole, who should be their two starter heading into the postseason, allowed seven home runs and nine earned runs in 11.1 IP. It was a ghastly set of performances, and it may have left the organization wondering how the rest of the season would shake out for their former Cy Young winner.
If there were any questions about Cole's abilities, his start against the 80-74 Arizona Diamondbacks may have alleviated a few worries. It may also have put to rest any internal debates. Cole did allow a home run this time out, but it was just one. Corbin Carroll pulled a 388-foot home run off Cole's bat at 110.7 MPH.
Headed into the postseason, pitching in Game 1 is an easy decision. Aaron Boone needs to hand the ball to Cy Young frontrunner and prospective MVP candidate Cam Schlittler. There's no reason to really overthink that one.
If Cole starts struggling again, though, the question of who the second starter is gets a little trickier. That might still be a conversation worth having if things go differently to close out the year, but for now, if Cole pitches the way he did against the Diamondbacks, there's no reason to save him for another series.
Cole's big test will be against the Tampa Bay Rays, since he lines up to face them in their next series. If he pitches well against them, he'll further solidify his spot as the team's two-starter.
A better outing for Gerrit Cole
When Aaron Boone was asked about Cole after the game, he said he wasn't too worried. He chalked his struggles up to a long season.
"I think a lot of people probably overreacted to a couple of outings that, frankly, are inevitable in a long season," Boone said, according to the New York Post's Greg Joyce. "The reality is he's having an outstanding season, he's throwing the ball really well, and a great pitcher like him is going to be able to make some adjustments when you have a couple where they get to you."
The Carroll blast was Cole's lone blemish. He pitched six innings of two-run ball, striking out six, allowing no walks, and four hits.
On the back end, he gave up a ton of soft contact. The Diamondbacks had an average exit velocity of 86.8 MPH against him. That's way down from his last two starts, when batters averaged 96.8 MPH against him.
This is the type of Cole the Yankees need in the postseason. Who knows what's happening with Aaron Judge, so the rotation and bullpen have to essentially be perfect if this team is going to make any noise this postseason.

For a historic franchise like the New York Yankees, rotation stability is paramount over the long haul of a 162-game season. That makes Cam Schlittler’s dominant breakout campaign all the more remarkable—so much so that manager Aaron Boone believes the young right-hander has built a compelling case to take home the American League Cy Young Award.
When asked about Schlittler’s transformative presence in the rotation, Boone didn’t mince words: “Well, he’s gonna win the Cy Young!” The manager’s ringing endorsement underscores just how dominant Schlittler has been on the mound this year.
While Boone continues to navigate rotation depth with Ryan Weathers sidelined for the remainder of the regular season, Schlittler gives the Yankees a legitimate ace to rely on as they gear up for October.
On the offensive side, Boone is also monitoring the return timeline for slugger Aaron Judge, who was sidelined with a calf strain. In the meantime, the Yankees skipper has relied on depth options like Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger to keep the lineup producing.
Key milestones driving Schlittler’s Cy Young case
A stellar 2026 breakout campaign with the Yankees has vaulted Schlittler directly into the front-runner conversation for the American League Cy Young Award. Stepping up as the de facto ace while Gerrit Cole missed time, Schlittler has delivered elite run suppression, swing-and-miss stuff, and exceptional durability.
Here is a breakdown of the key numbers and milestones anchoring Schlittler’s Cy Young candidacy:
- 1.95 ERA: Schlittler took over the MLB ERA lead in September, standing as the only qualified starter with an ERA under 2.00.
- Historical run: His 1.71 ERA through his first 16 starts marked the lowest ERA by a Yankees starter through that stretch since Hall of Famer Whitey Ford in 1964.
- 228 Strikeouts in 184.2 IP (11.1 K/9): Schlittler eclipsed the 200-strikeout mark on August 28 against Boston, becoming the fourth-youngest pitcher in franchise history to achieve the feat.
- Signature outings: Highlighted by a career-high 13-strikeout performance against the Cincinnati Reds on June 19, along with double-digit strikeout shutouts against Philadelphia (12 K) and Atlanta (11 K).
Other top Cy Young contenders
Schlittler isn’t running unopposed in a tightly contested American League race. Strong campaigns from power arm Dylan Cease of the Toronto Blue Jays and left-hander Garrett Crochet of the Boston Red Sox keep them firmly in the mix.
Over in the National League, the Cy Young field features plenty of heavy hitters, headlined by Milwaukee Brewers phenom Jacob Misiorowski, Atlanta Braves veteran Chris Sale, and the Philadelphia Phillies duo of Cristopher Sanchez and Jesus Luzardo.

New York Yankees pitcher Gerrit Cole still has a very big problem heading into the MLB playoffs.
Cole allowed four hits while registering six strikeouts, and his control remained sharp without any walks. He did surrender yet another home run, but for the most part, this was a solid outing by the right-hander.
Cole generated just six swings-and-misses on 62 strikes against the Diamondbacks, marking a 15 percent whiff rate. And while that was better than his eight percent rate against the New York Mets in his preceding start, it's still not good.
In fact, on the season as a whole, Cole has posted a 21.3 percent whiff rate, which places him in the 18th percentile in baseball.
Cole has been declining in that area for quite some time now, but this season has been particularly bad in that department.
Now, thanks to Cole's pinpoint control and his ability to paint corners, he still owns a 9.1 K/9 rate this year, a testament to just how good of a pitcher he is.
And while his average fastball velocity (96.8 mph) still ranks in the 85th percentile, his secondary stuff is simply not as lethal anymore.
Cole has still managed to log a 3.63 ERA in spite of his question marks this season, but the days of him being a bona fide ace appear to be over.
It also begs the question of whether or not he would be the Yankees' best option for a No. 2 starter in the playoffs. We know that Cam Schlittler will be the lead arm. But will Cole get the nod over Max Fried? An argument can even be made for Carlos Rodon, who has been very good when healthy this season.
Chances are, Aaron Boone will hand the No. 2 job to Cole because he's Gerrit Cole and because he has been good for most of 2026. But the fact that Cole's stuff is clearly declining — and right before the postseason — is a major concern.
Cole is smart enough where he can find ways to work around his ace stuff no longer being there. We just saw it in Arizona on Friday night. But can the Yankees trust him enough at this stage to get a pivotal Game 2 start?
We're about to find out.

PHOENIX — Cam Schlittler llega este sábado al Chase Field con otra oportunidad de convertir una temporada que ya es dominante en algo aún más difícil de alcanzar para el resto de la Liga Americana.
El lanzador diestro de los Yankees llega a su partido contra Arizona con un balance de 14-6, una efectividad de 1,95, un WHIP de 0,90 y 228 strikeouts en 184 2/3 entradas. Ha cedido una carrera o menos en siete salidas seguidas, una racha que le ha llevado de ser un simple aspirante a situarse en el centro de las conversaciones sobre el premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, mientras que los Yankees se han asegurado otra plaza en la postemporada.
El contraste con su rival más cercano se acentuó el viernes por la noche sin que Schlittler lanzara ni una sola bola. El as de Toronto, Dylan Cease , solo aguantó 2 2/3 entradas en la derrota por 7-1 ante Texas. Concedió seis bases por bolas, encajó cuatro carreras (solo una limpia) y solo 36 de sus 74 lanzamientos fueron strikes. Sportsnet también midió su bola rápida a 93,6 mph, 3,3 mph por debajo de su media de la temporada.
Cease sigue teniendo una temporada de élite. Tras la derrota, tiene un balance de 11-6, con una ERA de 2,40, un WHIP de 1,10 y 239 strikeouts en 169 entradas, lo que le sitúa a la cabeza de la Liga Americana. Su total de ponches sigue siendo mejor que el de Schlittler. Sin embargo, su promedio de carreras limpias, la eficiencia en su carga de trabajo y su control reciente marcan ahora un contraste estadístico más marcado, justo en el momento en que las opiniones sobre los premios se van consolidando.
Para los Yankees, eso va más allá de los trofeos. Schlittler se ha convertido en el miembro más estable de un cuerpo de lanzadores de los Yankees que ha tenido que lidiar con las ausencias de Gerrit Cole, Max Fried y Carlos Rodón. Además, está previsto que sea el primero en lanzar en la rotación de Nueva York en octubre, lo que hace que sus últimas salidas en la temporada regular cobren importancia tanto para la lucha por los playoffs como para la carrera por los premios.
Los Yankees llegan al sábado con un balance de 89-64, a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay, así que cada salida que le queda sigue teniendo un interés inmediato más allá de la carrera por los premios.
Una votación unánime cambia el panorama de la carrera
Esta semana ha llegado la señal más clara hasta ahora. En la última votación del premio Cy Young de la temporada en MLB.com, los 32 votantes eligieron al as de los Yankees como el número uno de la Liga Americana. Consiguió el máximo de 160 puntos. Cease quedó segundo con 126.
El jurado pidió a los votantes que clasificaran a cinco lanzadores en una escala del 5 al 1 (5-4-3-2-1), teniendo en cuenta tanto lo que había pasado como cómo podrían desarrollarse las dos últimas semanas. Esa distinción es importante. La encuesta no es la votación oficial de la BBWAA y no decide el premio, pero la unanimidad entre los 32 votantes de MLB.com muestra lo mucho que ha subido la posición del as de los Yankees.
El último modelo de premios de ESPN apunta en la misma dirección. Su sistema AXE sitúa a Schlittler en primer lugar entre los lanzadores de la Liga Americana con 153,1, por delante de Cease, que tiene 145,8. ESPN señaló que Schlittler ya llevaba un balance de 12-6 con una efectividad de 2,09 hasta agosto, y que luego empezó septiembre con un 2-0 y una efectividad de 0,89 en sus tres primeras salidas del mes.
El caso de Cone explica por qué los números tienen más peso
David Cone ha definido el valor de Schlittler basándose en algo más sencillo que una fórmula para los premios. El exganador del premio Cy Young de los Yankees destacó la constancia con la que este lanzador diestro ha aliviado la presión de anotar sobre la alineación y el bullpen.
«¿Dónde estarían los Yankees sin él?», dijo Cone.
A continuación, Cone situó a Schlittler al mismo nivel que las estrellas más valiosas de la liga al hablar de lo mucho que Nueva York ha dependido de él a lo largo de una temporada marcada por los cambios constantes en la rotación.
«Schlittler está entre los mejores. Se lo merece, sin duda hay que tenerlo muy en cuenta», dijo Cone.
Ese argumento viene respaldado por la trayectoria de Schlittler esta temporada. Cone señaló esta semana que el lanzador diestro ya había hecho 21 salidas en las que solo había cedido cero o una carrera. En las últimas siete salidas de Schlittler, las estadísticas actuales de la MLB muestran una efectividad de 1,00 en 45 entradas, con 57 ponches y un WHIP de 0,76.
El tropiezo de Cease marca la diferencia en los últimos compases
Lo más revelador es el momento en que se hizo la encuesta. La encuesta de MLB.com se publicó antes de la salida más corta de Cease esta temporada, el viernes en Arlington. Eso significa que el resultado unánime no necesitó su último tropiezo para diferenciar a los dos lanzadores.
Las estadísticas de Cease siguen siendo lo suficientemente buenas como para que la carrera siga siendo reñida. Tiene 11 strikeouts más que Schlittler en 15 2/3 entradas menos. Pero también ha concedido 78 bases por bolas frente a las 44 de Schlittler, y el viernes fue la tercera salida consecutiva en la que Cease no logró completar seis entradas.
Schlittler tendrá la próxima oportunidad de demostrar su valía. Los Yankees lo alinearán contra Brandon Pfaadt el sábado, con Nueva York con un balance de 89-64, a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana y con la clasificación para la postemporada ya asegurada. Una buena actuación no garantizaría oficialmente el premio, pero dejaría aún menos margen para que algún rival cambie el panorama de esta recta final de la temporada.
Queda una última prueba antes de octubre
A los Yankees aún les queda más de una semana antes de que termine la temporada regular, y los aficionados de los Yankees saben que las votaciones para los premios no se basan en encuestas de predicción. Una o dos malas salidas finales aún pueden cambiar el panorama. Esa es la incertidumbre que Schlittler debe afrontar.
Lo que ha cambiado es la carga de la prueba. Schlittler ya no tiene que esforzarse por meterse en la conversación. Las últimas medidas a nivel nacional ya lo han situado al frente, mientras que el mal viernes de Cease ha hecho que la carrera sea aún más dura.
El sábado en Arizona le da al as de los Yankees otra oportunidad de ampliar aún más esa ventaja.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.content:encoded:
In the absence of Shohei Ohtani and Aaron Judge, the mysterious power outages of Vlad Guerrero Jr. and Cal Raleigh, and the injuries to Tarik Skubal and Garrett Crochet, baseball’s postseason awards are coming into focus by ushering in a new wave of 20-something superstars.
Going into the weekend the teams with the best records in each league were the small market Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays, both of which with leading candidates for baseball’s postseason hardware who are still years away from their prime.
For the Brewers, 24-year-old Jacob Misiorowski is the runaway leader for the NL Cy Young Award, at 15-5 and leading the majors in ERA (1.89), strikeouts (243), WHIP (0.812) and strikeouts per nine innings (13.1) — while the Rays, in their bid to salt away the AL East, have gotten a late boost from their 23-year old third baseman Junior Caminero, who took over the AL home run lead last week and was neck and neck with Houston’s Yordan Alvarez in RBI and total bases.
On the surface, Alvarez, who leads the NL in OPS and batting (.311), would appear to have the overall statistical edge on Caminero for the MVP. But the fact that Alvarez is a DH and Caminero, who’s missed only one game while adding superior defense at third base for a team that is likely to win the division also bodes well for him. This is one race that figures to go down to the last day, with the deciding factor possibly being whether the Astros win the AL West.
As for the AL Cy Young Award, Cam Schlittler, the Yankees’ 25-year-old sophomore, has zoomed ahead of the Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease with a season for the ages, including a major league-leading 1.95 ERA and 0.904 WHIP and the most starts in Yankee history allowing one or fewer runs (21). His 1.14 ERA for 16 road starts is also the lowest in American League history.
Over in the National League, with Ohtani shackled with knee and bicep injuries that have prevented him from pitching since July 3, effectively ending his chances for a fourth straight MVP, the Cubs’ 24-year-old Pete Crow-Armstrong has stepped up with a phenomenal breakthrough season. Going into the weekend, Crow-Armstrong, who’s played every game, was leading the majors in slugging, OPS and total bases and was second behind Kyle Schwarber in the NL in homers with 44 and third in RBI with 105. On Aug. 29 he hit three homers in a game and with his 44th homer on Sept. 17 surpassed Hall of Famer Billy Williams as the most by a left-handed hitter in Cubs history.
Sorry, but we’re again unable to refrain from reminding that Crow-Armstrong was the Mets’ 2020 first round draft pick who, the next season, they traded to the Cubs for two months of rental free agent Javy Baez.
When it comes to the Rookies of the Year, I realize in this lost season for the Mets there’s been a lot of buzz for Nolan McLean and Carson Benge, but neither are going to win the NL award. That would have to be Cincinnati’s unsung Sal Stewart, who even if nobody probably had him on their Rookie of the Year bingo card at the start of the season, happens to be leading all NL rookies in homers (32) and RBI (110) and has played every day. An equally strong favorite for the AL Rookie of the Year is Cleveland lefty Parker Messick, a second round draft pick out of Florida State three years ago, who leads all AL rookies in wins (12), ERA (2.57), strikeouts (186) and WHIP (1.04).
IT’S A MADD, MADD WORLD
You have to wonder if the window has already closed on Aaron Judge leading the Yankees to a World Series title. The 34-year-old Yankee captain has missed 317 games (and counting) and had only four full seasons since 2018 and the fact remains he’s 280 pounds — and every time he has to make a diving catch or crash into a wall at his age now that’s 280 pounds of impact on his body. No surprise the rib injury that’s sidelined him most of this season. … For nine decades, Juan Vene was a fixture in the press boxes of Yankee Stadium and Shea Stadium and even though his name may not be familiar to most New York baseball fans, he was a legend, especially in his native Venezuela, but really all over Latin America. Word came last week that Vene passed away Sept. 15 in Miami at age 97. A long-time member of the Baseball Writers Association and a regular Hall of Fame voter, Vene was a friend to all of us. Anyone needing an interview with a Latin player in the offseason could count on Vene to help set it up. RIP. … If the White Sox are somehow able to hold on and win the AL Central it will be a remarkable achievement given the year-long state of their starting pitching. According to the Elias Bureau, White Sox starters have logged by far the fewest innings (639) in the majors to the runner-up Nationals’ 671 1/3, and as they stagger to the finish line they have been employing “openers” 2-3 times a week.

The New York Yankees will play the rest of the regular season without slugger Aaron Judge. While they understand the magnitude of his loss, they enter the stretch run with belief.
The Yanks scored five runs in the first inning of a 9-2 victory over the Arizona Diamondbacks in the first game of a weekend series Friday, and the teams meet again Saturday in Phoenix as Arizona attempts to stay alive in the National League wild-card race.
"Obviously losing 'Judgey' hurts," Cody Bellinger said. "We all know he's the best hitter in the game. For us in here, our mindset is we're going to have to find a way. The talent in this room speaks for itself.
"I'm fully confident we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win and beat anybody."
American League Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA) will face Arizona right-hander Brandon Pfaadt (7-3, 3.77) in the second game of the series.
The Diamondbacks (80-74) will ask Pfaadt to end a slump in which they have lost five of six. They are five games behind San Diego, the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia (all 85-69) for the three NL wild-card spots with eight games to play.
"We know where we're at," Arizona manager Torey Lovullo said. "We can't afford to worry about things we can't control. I'm going to say there's time. There's always time."
The Yankees (89-64) are 48-39 this season without Judge, who was placed on the injured list Friday with a strained right calf after missing three months earlier with a fractured right rib.
New York is also without injured regulars Jazz Chisholm Jr. (thumb) and Trent Grisham (hamstring), although manager Aaron Boone said Chisholm could return for the Tampa Bay series early next week.
The Yankees, who already have qualified for the postseason, are four games behind Tampa Bay in the AL East, and the teams have a four-game series at Yankee Stadium beginning Tuesday.
"There is no replacing a player as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations that don't change now," Boone said. "One thing we do know is that we are in the dance.
"We've been built on the strength of our starting pitching all year."
No one has been as strong as Schlittler, who is in his first full season and has made every start while Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon have missed time with injuries or recovery time.
Schlittler has won four of his last five starts and has given up one run or fewer in each of his last seven. He was struck on the back of his right leg by Bo Bichette's 111.5 mph comebacker on his 94th and last pitch of a 2-0 victory over the New York Mets last Sunday, but shrugged it off.
"You have an ace at the top that has pitched like that," Boone said. "That's a good place to start. He's been dominant. This is largely in line with who we saw down the stretch last year."
Schlittler has never faced the Diamondbacks, although Jesus Sanchez is 4 for 12 with three walks against him.
Pfaadt is 0-2 with a 5.74 ERA in his last five starts, and he gave up six runs and 10 hits in 6 2/3 innings in a loss to Texas on Aug. 12. He will be pitching on six days' rest after being pushed back so Eduardo Rodriguez could start the first game of the series.
Pfaadt lost his only outing against the Yankees, giving up six runs in 4 1/3 innings of a 7-1 loss as a rookie in 2023. Cody Bellinger is 2 for 7 with two solo homers against him and Luis Garcia Jr. is 3 for 7 with a homer.
