Yankees news: Gerrit Cole makes history in win vs. Diamondbacks appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
New York Yankees starter Gerrit Cole made MLB history in Friday night's 9-2 win against the Arizona Diamondbacks at Chase Field.
The 36-year-old earned his 162nd career victory, moving past Mike Moore's 161 wins for the most ever by a pitcher who was selected No. 1 overall in the MLB Draft. Cole was chosen first by the Pittsburgh Pirates in 2011, while Moore went to the Seattle Mariners with the top selection in 1981. David Price is next on the list, ranking third with 157 career wins.
The milestone came as Cole bounced back after allowing seven home runs across his previous two starts, the highest two-game figure of his career. He also had surrendered leadoff home runs in each of those outings.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
After working on his delivery and potential pitch-tipping issues since his previous start against the New York Mets, Cole retired Arizona in order during a 12-pitch opening inning. Corbin Carroll later hit a two-run homer on a four-seam fastball that missed its location, but Cole gave up nothing else to the Diamondbacks.
The right-hander completed six innings, allowing two runs and four hits while issuing no walks and striking out six. He threw 90 pitches, with 62 going for strikes, finishing with a 9-9 record.
New York provided Cole with plenty of early support, sending its first five hitters to base against Eduardo Rodriguez during a five-run opening inning. Ben Rice drew a bases-loaded walk, Amed Rosario delivered an RBI single and George Lombard Jr. added a two-run single.
Rice later launched his 39th homer of the season in the third inning, while Lombard hit his own solo shot in the sixth and finished with three RBIs.
The Yankees improved to 89-64 and moved within four games of the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East with nine games remaining. New York had already secured a postseason berth and has now won 11 of its last 15 games.
Manager Aaron Boone also confirmed that Cole should receive a start if the Yankees reach the American League Wild Card Series.

item.content:encoded:
Even the biggest of homers couldn’t predict just how dominant Cam Schlittler would be this season. The ace of the New York Yankees has cemented himself as one of the top pitchers in all of baseball and proven that last year was not a fluke. Schlittler’s 2026 season may even go down as one of the best pitching performances in the entire history of the franchise. Despite the Yankees’ storied franchise, only six pitchers have won the Cy Young award for the team. Schlittler is likely about to change that.
With 6.0 fWAR accumulated throughout the 2026 season, Schlittler is tied with Milwaukee Brewers’ sensation Jacob Misiorowski for the league lead among pitchers. It’s no coincidence that both hurlers are the favorites to take home the Cy Young in their respective leagues. For Schlittler, he’d not only be the seventh Yankees pitcher to win the award, but he’d also be the youngest.
As the Yankees prepare for another postseason run, they will hope that Schlittler’s historic performance is able to carry over into October. As history has taught us, the Yankees win when their pitchers win.
Yankees Complete History of Cy Young Award Winners
It’s hard to fathom that the Yankees only average a Cy Young award winner every 20 years or so. From Mike Mussina to CC Sabathia, the franchise has certainly featured plenty of Hall of Fame pitchers that have come close to winning the award. Mussina was overshadowed by teammate Roger Clemens during his stellar 2001 campaign with the Yankees. Sabathia got as close to third place in the voting following his 2010 season.
Even the great Mariano Rivera couldn’t quite do enough to sway the voters and win the elusive award as a reliever. He finished in the top three of voting four separate times. This includes two seasons when he finished in the top 10 of the MVP race. It’s rare, but pitchers have occasionally made strong cases for MVP.
We’ll detail the six previous Yankees who actually managed to cross the finish line and why they deserved to take home the top pitching award. And because a Yankees season isn’t complete without a World Series title, we’ll also note how far a Cy Young winner got the team in the postseason.
Gerrit Cole, 2023
As the most recent Yankees pitcher to win the award, Gerrit Cole did something in 2023 that only one other player had accomplished in the team’s history, winning the award by unanimous decision. With all 30 first place votes, Cole more than doubled the amount of points that second-place pitcher Sonny Gray received.
As you might imagine, Cole’s 2023 is his most impressive season with the Yankees since joining the club in 2020. He struck out 222 hitters across 209 innings pitched. Although his 3.16 FIP doesn’t scream “elite pitcher,” he allowed just 157 hits while surrendering just 48 walks.
Despite Cole’s brilliance, the club finished with a mediocre 82-80 record, missing out on the playoffs for the first time since the 2016 season, though you couldn’t blame Cole for that. He boasted a 1.03 ERA and a minuscule 0.686 WHIP over his last five starts of the season, including a two-hit shutdown against the Toronto Blue Jays in his last start of the season. If only Aaron Judge hadn't run toe-first into the wall at Dodger Stadium.
Roger Clemens, 2001
As mentioned earlier, Clemens scooped away a lot of votes from Mussina when he won the Cy Young in 2001. Some would argue that Clemens probably stole that award, but you can’t deny that he still had a very good season.
With more emphasis placed on individual wins back then, Clemens boasted 20 wins to go alongside his 213 strikeouts. Clemens’ 2001 season would probably be considered his weakest of his seven award-winning seasons. But hey, it was the early 2000s. People voted more on vibes than actual performance.
Clemens’ 3.29 FIP that season was enough to help take the Yankees to the World Series, where they lost in heartbreaking fashion to the Arizona Diamondbacks. But we don’t have to dwell on that part.
Ron Guidry, 1978
Before Clemens won the award in 2001, it had been 23 years since a Yankees pitcher won it. But oh man, did Ron Guidry ever earn the award in 1978. With a 1.74 ERA across 273 1/3 innings pitched, his season is what many consider to be the best by a pitcher in team history. His home run per nine rate of 0.4 is almost laughable.
Even by modern metrics, Guidry was the clear-cut winner that season. His 2.19 FIP and 208 ERA+ was leaps and bounds better than any other pitcher up for consideration that year, which is why he became the first Yankees pitcher to win the award unanimously.
Guidry was a large reason that the team won 100 games that year. The Yankees would carry that tremendous momentum into the postseason and defeat the Los Angeles Dodgers in the World Series.
Sparky Lyle, 1977
Unlike the long wait in between Clemens and Guidry winning the Cy Young, the Yankees actually had quite the time in the late 70s when it came to award-winning pitchers. Before Guidry, the team saw reliever Sparky Lyle take home the award in 1977. He became just the second reliever in MLB history to win the honor. Since then, seven more relievers have joined the rare club.
When looking at his numbers, you probably wouldn’t really consider Lyle to be a dominant force out of the bullpen. Despite that, he was certainly one of the most effective pitchers in the league. With just 68 strikeouts in 137 innings, Lyle didn’t just rely on swing and misses to get outs. He collected 13 wins and 26 saves, demonstrating just how pivotal he was to the Yankees.
With Lyle coming out of the pen, the Yankees won 100 games in the regular season. He then helped pave the way to a World Series title over the Dodgers.
Whitey Ford, 1961
With 236 career wins and six World Series rings in his collection, Whitey Ford is one of the foremost Yankees winners in team history. In 1961, he added a Cy Young to his trophy case. At 32 years old, he threw a career-high 283 innings, which included 11 complete games and three shutouts.
Ford’s 1961 season may be outshined in the annals of history by Roger Maris’ record-setting performance, but that doesn’t make it any less impressive. Like other pitchers on this list, Ford didn’t put up mind-boggling numbers or boast off-the-charts metrics. Outside of innings pitched, he didn’t really do one thing extremely well. However, he did do just about everything very well.
Ford was more than enough of a pitcher to be considered the ace of a team that some argue to be one of the best teams in MLB history. With 109 wins and a World Series title, it is hard to argue against that claim.
Bob Turley, 1958
Just three years before Ford won his Cy Young, Bob Turley became the first Yankees pitcher to win the award in 1958. Once again, like a number of other Yankees on this list, Turley’s 1958 season isn’t something that you would circle as an all-time great year. His 4.04 WHIP and 119 ERA+ were shockingly poor in hindsight.
Turley probably became the first Yankees pitcher to steal the award from a more deserving pitcher as well. Sorry, Warren Spahn. While Turley threw 245 1/3 innings, including 19 complete games, he was an especially wild pitcher. Turley walked 128 batters, nearly double the amount of walks surrendered by the second and third place pitchers in the Cy Young voting combined that year.
With all of that said, Turley pitched well enough to help lead the Yankees to 92 wins. They then went on to defeat the Milwaukee Braves in seven games in the World Series. When all is said and done, what more could you ask for?

PHOENIX — Just in case anyone thought the New York Yankees would simply fade away into the night, their season drifting out to sea with the news that Aaron Judge may be done for the season, the Bronx Bombers delivered a subtle message Friday night that reverberated around the baseball world.
The Yankees, with Gerrit Cole looking more like the 2023 Cy Young winner than the pitcher who looked like he was throwing batting practice earlier this month, smacked around the Arizona Diamondbacks 9-2 Friday, and acted afterwards as if it was simply business as usual.
There was Cole, who had given up seven homers in his last two starts pitching his best game in a month, yielding four hits and two runs in six innings.
There was DH Ben Rice, looking like a top-5 MVP candidate by hitting his 39th home run of the season − just as Yankees manager Aaron Boone predicted in spring training − to go along with 94 RBI.
There was rookie shortstop George Lombard, hitting a homer and playing flawless defense.
And there were the Yankees, talking as if they plan to be playing deep into October, whether Judge is in uniform or on their bench as a cheerleader. Judge is going on the injured list with a strained calf and the Yankees have no idea whether he'll return.
"I mean, it's a tough blow for us to take,'' Rice said. "Obviously, we were missing him for a long time there (three months), so this one is especially hard to swallow, just being back for a brief period and already gone.
"But we got no choice but to just keep playing hard, keeping doing our thing.''
Well, that starts on the mound, and with Cole dominating Friday, with Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler scheduled Saturday, and Max Fried and Carlos Rodon pitching well, there may not be a more formidable starting rotation in the postseason.
Cole, 9-9 with a 3.63 ERA in his first season back from Tommy John surgery, certainly knows there's room for improvement. But after being belted around with a 7.15 ERA his past two starts, giving up seven homers and 15 hits in 11.1 innings, this was a massive improvement.
"I thought he was really good,'' Boone said. "You know he grinded pretty hard. Between the last start and this one, there are subtle adjustments you make that a lot of people probably over-reacted to.
"The reality is he's having an outstanding season. He's throwing the ball really well, and a great pitcher like him is going to be able to make some adjustments.''
Cole, who missed the entire 2025 season and the first 51 games this year, says he modified his mechanics to remake his delivery. Why, except for missing his location on a low fastball to Corbin Carroll in the second inning, resulting in a two-run homer, he was on-point with virtually all of his other pitches. He threw 90 pitches − 62 for strikes − without walking a batter.
"I mean, I don't think we did a perfect job tonight,'' Cole said. "I think we moved the needle in the right direction. I think there's some meat on the bone there. It's not easy, but it's necessary. It's the big leagues.''
Yep, just like no one is going to feel sorry for the Yankees with the loss of Judge. Not the Tampa Bay Rays, who are still in first place with a four-game lead. Not the Boston Red Sox, who the Yankees likely will face in the first round. Not a soul outside the Yankees organization.
"We have a lot of confidence in here,'' Cole said. "I mean, for the most part of the summer, we've been tested really, really hard, and responded − by and large − really well.
"We have a lot of perfectionists in here. We're always trying to be perfect, and always striving to be the best. But the reality is we've had a lot of obstacles that we've had to overcome, and we've played really well. So we're looking forward to more challenges to come.''
Yes, with or without Judge. The Yankees went 46-39 when he was out 100 days with a rib fracture, and they believe they're built for October. They know they have four top-quality starters and a deep bullpen that can dominate anyone.
"That's probably our biggest strength,'' Boone said. "Whoever we hand the ball to every day, we know is going to give us an opportunity to win a game.''
They proved that this night, with Judge merely watching from the bench, knowing he may have played his final game of the season.
"We're obviously bummed for Aaron, and Aaron's probably bummed too,'' Cole said, "but we've been in this position before this year. Unfortunately, it's our reality at this point.''

PHOENIX — With Gerrit Cole fresh off two rough outings, Aaron Boone quieted conversation over whether the longtime ace should get a postseason start, especially if the second-place Yankees find themselves in a best-of-three Wild Card series.
Asked if Cole would be guaranteed a start in the Wild Card round, the likeliest scenario for the Yankees, the manager replied with a sly smile on Friday.
“I would expect Gerrit Cole to start, yes,” Boone said before the righty started the Bombers’ 9-2, series-opening win over the Diamondbacks.
While the skipper was not completely definitive, Yankees pitching coach Matt Blake noted that Cole is lined up to pitch in the Wild Card round, which begins Sept. 29. As things stand, the Yankees would host the Red Sox, who have hit Cole well throughout his career.
Blake added that the Yankees have yet to formally discuss their postseason rotation plans, which also have to account for Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler, Max Fried and Carlos Rodón.
As a future Hall of Famer and the 2023 American League Cy Young, it would be shocking if Cole was not tabbed for a postseason start. However, the question was posed to Boone after Cole surrendered nine earned runs and seven homers over 16.2 innings in his previous two games against the Padres and Mets. Even prior to that, strikeouts and swing-and-miss had been hard to come by for Cole.
The 36-year-old, now 21 starts removed from Tommy John surgery, entered Friday with a 21.6 Whiff%, his lowest since 2016, and a 24.6 K%, his lowest since 2017. While he proceeded to strike out six D-Backs batters, he only induced six whiffs on 41 swings and 90 pitches.
Still, the evening represented a bounce-back start for Cole. After working to tighten up his delivery and improve his deception on the mound, the veteran completed six innings while also totaling four hits, two earned runs, zero walks and five hard-hit balls. The only runs Cole permitted came on a two-run, second-inning homer from Corbin Carroll, who smoked a 97.3-mph fastball that missed its spot.
Cole’s four-seamer had been a problem for him in his last two starts, yielding just six whiffs while being the target of 15 hard-hit balls.
While Cole was certainly better on Friday, his fastball and swing-and-miss woes are still something to keep an eye on with him scheduled to get one more regular season start. Blake said the latter can be attributed to “a host of things,” including Cole’s sequencing, command and the lack of deception that he worked on.
“I don’t think we did a perfect job tonight,” Cole said of his delivery. “I think we moved the needle in the right direction, but there’s still some meat on the bone there.”
Blake also noted that Cole hasn’t left the strike zone to get chase when given the opportunity in two-strike counts. Cole shared the same thought after his last start against the Mets.
One non-factor, according to Boone, Blake and Cole, is fatigue. All three have said that there is no reason to think Cole’s surgically repaired arm is tired, and he has said that he feels fine physically.
“Obviously, he’s getting up to the innings threshold we talked about in the beginning of the year, but he seems to be responding well,” Blake said. “The ball’s coming out with similar life, and the metrics are in line, so that doesn’t seem to be the case.”
With Friday’s game in the books, Cole has now logged 121.1 innings this season. With a 3.63 ERA, he’s put together a strong body of work after missing the entire 2025 season.
Boone, however, insisted Cole has had a “great” season before Friday’s win, and he took it a step further afterward.
“A lot of people probably overreacted to a couple of outings that, frankly, are inevitable in a long season. The reality is, he’s having an outstanding season,” Boone said. “He’s throwing the ball really well and a great pitcher like him is going to be able to make some adjustments when you have a couple where they get to you.”
While that’s an exaggeration by Cole’s lofty standards, one thing is certain with the playoffs nearing.
“He’s going to be a heavy factor for us,” Blake said.

Phoenix, Arizona.- Ben Rice conectó su jonrón número 39 de la temporada, Gerrit Cole se convirtió en la selección número 1 del draft con más victorias y los Yankees de Nueva York usaron una primera entrada de cinco carreras para tomar el control temprano y vencer a los Diamondbacks de Arizona 9-2 el viernes por la noche.
Tras enterarse de que Aaron Judge, tres veces Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana, regresaría a la lista de lesionados por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha, los Yankees consiguieron su octava victoria en 10 partidos. Nueva York, que ya tiene asegurado un puesto en los playoffs, se encuentra a cuatro juegos de los Tampa Bay Rays en la División Este de la Liga Americana a falta de nueve partidos.
Los Diamondbacks han perdido tres partidos seguidos y sus esperanzas de playoffs están en serio peligro. Están a cinco juegos del último puesto de comodín de la Liga Nacional con ocho partidos restantes.
Los primeros cinco bateadores de Nueva York llegaron a base contra el lanzador zurdo All-Star de los Diamondbacks, Eduardo Rodríguez, y un sencillo de dos carreras de George Lombard Jr. puso el marcador 5-0. Lombard añadió un jonrón solitario en la sexta entrada y terminó con tres carreras impulsadas.
Cole (9-9) se recuperó de dos aperturas en las que permitió siete jonrones, la mayor cantidad que ha permitido en dos juegos. Permitió dos carreras y cuatro hits en seis entradas, ponchando a seis bateadores.
Seleccionado en primer lugar por Pittsburgh en 2011, Cole ganó su partido número 162. Eso es uno más que Mike Moore, elegido en primer lugar por Seattle en 1981.
Rodríguez (15-7) eligió un mal momento para tener posiblemente su peor apertura de la temporada, necesitando 45 lanzamientos para conseguir tres outs, su mayor cantidad en una primera entrada. Permitió siete carreras, cinco hits y cuatro bases por bolas en 5 1/3 entradas.
Corbin Carroll conectó un jonrón de dos carreras para reducir la desventaja a 5-2 en la segunda entrada. El jonrón solitario de Rice en la tercera puso a los Yankees arriba 6-2.
A continuación
Los D-backs envían al lanzador derecho Brandon Pfaadt (7-3, 3.77 ERA) al montículo el sábado por la noche, mientras que los Yankees responden con el lanzador derecho Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95).
Información: AP.

PHOENIX — Dos noches antes, la pelota se le había escapado por debajo del guante y había contribuido a que los Yankees cayeran derrotados en un partido de 13 entradas. El novato se lo tomó muy a pecho. El viernes, George Lombard Jr. respondió de la única forma en que puede hacerlo un jugador joven: con un bate lo suficientemente contundente como para ahogar ese recuerdo.
Conectó un sencillo de dos carreras en la primera entrada. Se llevó un jonrón en la sexta. Al final de la noche, sumaba dos hits y tres carreras impulsadas, y el campocorto que parecía desconcertado en Minnesota se mostraba ahora como una pieza clave del equipo.
La coincidencia fue casi cruel por su simetría. La misma tarde en que el equipo se preparaba para recibir el golpe más duro por una lesión en meses, su jugador titular menos consolidado cuajó su partido más sólido.
Lo que podría haber sido un golpe bajo se convirtió en toda una declaración de intenciones. Y esa declaración no tuvo casi nada que ver con el hombre por el que todos estaban preocupados.
Los Yankees arrollaron a los Diamondbacks por 9-2 en el Chase Field el viernes por la noche, unas horas después de enterarse de que Aaron Judge volvería a la lista de lesionados por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha que podría poner fin a su temporada regular. Nueva York mejoró su balance a 89-64, sumó su undécima victoria en 15 partidos y se colocó a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, después de que los Rays perdieran 4-2 ante Boston. Los Yankees también mantuvieron una ventaja de 5 partidos y medio sobre los Red Sox por el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
Una primera entrada de cinco carreras en la que no hizo falta ninguna superestrella
El modelo a seguir para una vida sin Judge quedó claro enseguida. Los Yankees enviaron a 10 bateadores al plato contra el zurdo de Arizona, Eduardo Rodríguez, y anotaron cinco veces antes de que se produjera el segundo out.
Los cinco primeros bateadores llegaron a base. Paul Goldschmidt consiguió una base por bolas , Cody Bellinger conectó un sencillo y, tras otra base por bolas, Ben Rice consiguió una base por bolas con las bases llenas, lo que permitió anotar una carrera. Amed Rosario conectó un sencillo de un toque que impulsó una carrera, un pase fallido permitió que Heliot Ramos anotara y Lombard conectó un sencillo de dos carreras por el centro para poner el 5-0 en el marcador.
No fue un solo golpe fulminante. Fueron nueve bateadores que obligaron a un ex All-Star a lanzar 45 veces en la primera entrada. Esa paciencia es el tipo de ataque que más necesitarán los Yankees en octubre, cuando la ausencia de Judge convierta cada remontada en un esfuerzo colectivo.
Cole se recompone y luego hace historia
La ventaja le permitió a Gerrit Cole respirar tranquilo. El lanzador diestro había encajado siete jonrones en sus dos últimas salidas, y se habían intensificado los rumores sobre si estaría listo para octubre. Con esta actuación, acalló gran parte de esos rumores.
Cole encajó un jonrón de dos carreras de Corbin Carroll en la segunda entrada, de nuevo con una bola rápida que se quedó en el plato, pero nada más. Lanzó seis entradas, cedió dos carreras con cuatro hits, no concedió ninguna base por bolas y ponchó a seis con 90 lanzamientos. Boone había dicho antes del partido que Cole sería el abridor en la serie de comodín de todas formas.
Cole se tomó esta salida como un paso adelante, no como una solución definitiva. Explicó que había dedicado el tiempo entre sus salidas a afinar su lanzamiento para mejorar su capacidad de engaño.
«No creo que lo hayamos hecho perfecto esta noche, pero sí que hemos dado un paso en la dirección correcta», dijo Cole. «Creo que todavía nos queda mucho por hacer. No es fácil, pero es necesario. Así son las grandes ligas».
Esta victoria fue la número 162 de la carrera de Cole, lo que le permitió superar a Mike Moore como el lanzador con más victorias de todos los tiempos entre los elegidos en primera posición en el draft de la MLB, un hito discreto en una noche llena de otros titulares.
Un error defensivo que se corrigió al instante
Esta es la jugada que da forma a la noche, y en la que pocos se fijarán. El error de Lombard dos días antes en Minnesota había formado parte de una secuencia decisiva que le costó a los Yankees un partido que podían haber ganado. El viernes se presentó algo que el deporte rara vez concede tan rápido: una segunda oportunidad sin condiciones.
Su jonrón en la sexta entrada sacó a Rodríguez del partido y amplió la ventaja a 7-2. Para un novato que se vio obligado a ocupar el puesto de campocorto en la recta final, su reacción importó más que las carreras. Cuando le preguntaron por la noche, Lombard lo dejó claro.
«Fue genial desde el principio, todos hicimos buenos turnos al bate», dijo Lombard. «Obviamente, había un buen lanzador en el montículo. Le hicimos trabajar».
Esta actuación llega justo cuando los Yankees están valorando los roles para la postemporada en el cuadro, donde la solidez de un novato ahora tiene un peso real de cara a octubre.
Rice se acerca a los 40 mientras Judge se queda en el banquillo
Rice le dio a los Yankees otro pilar. Su jonrón en la tercera entrada contra Rodríguez recorrió 390 pies y fue el número 39 de la temporada, una cifra que, según el entrenador Aaron Boone, ya había predicho en los entrenamientos de primavera. Rice terminó con ese jonrón y un triple, y suma cinco jonrones en sus últimos 22 partidos.
El ambiente en torno a ese swing era sombrío. Judge había impulsado tantas primeras entradas a lo largo de los años, y ahora los Yankees tienen que volver a luchar por llegar a octubre sin él. Rice se refirió a lo difícil que resulta este momento.
«Es un duro golpe para nosotros», dijo Rice. «Llevábamos mucho tiempo echándole de menos, así que esto nos cuesta especialmente aceptarlo. Pero no nos queda más remedio que seguir jugando a tope y seguir haciendo lo nuestro».
Los Yankees creen que el pitcheo les llevará a la victoria pase lo que pase. Cam Schlittler, el probable ganador del Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, está previsto que sea el abridor en un posible primer partido de la ronda de comodines, con Max Fried y Carlos Rodón como relevos.
Nueva York y Arizona vuelven a enfrentarse este sábado, con Schlittler listo para medirse a Brandon Pfaadt. La inminente serie de cuatro partidos contra los Rays en el Yankee Stadium, que empieza el martes con una doble jornada, podría decidir el título de la división. Por una noche, un novato algo desconcertado y un as que se mantuvo firme hicieron que los Yankees parecieran listos.

MLB Trade Rumors | Darragh McDonald: Well, it was nice while it lasted. The Yankees announced yesterday evening that they will be placing right fielder Aaron Judge on the ten-day injured list with a calf strain today; Max Schuemann is expected to be the corresponding move. Since it will be backdated to the 16th, Judge will be eligible to come off the IL for the final day of the season; however, given the nature of calf strains, it is entirely possible that we have seen the last of No. 99 for 2026.
New York Daily News | Gary Phillips: Arguably the biggest surprise of the 2026 season — beyond the fact that the Yankees somehow managed to keep their heads above water despite Aaron Judge missing three months, of course — has been the breakout of outfielder Spencer Jones. The former top prospect has managed to position himself as “a key cog in the Yankees’ lineup,” taking advantage of opportunities offered by injuries to Judge, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, and Giancarlo Stanton. In particular, his performance against southpaws, which had long been a weakness throughout his minor league career, has been a pleasant surprise. That being said, it hasn’t been all sunshine and roses: Jones has yet to flash the leather in the way many have expected him to. Even so, however, it seems likely that Jones will be a critical part of the team’s postseason run, whether as the starting center fielder or a key reserve.
MLB.com | Mike Lupica: For all the attention that the Yankees’ veteran stars — Judge, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, and Giancarlo Stanton — receive, the 2026 season has been a veritable youth movement. Key to that has been the development, of course, of first baseman/designated hitter Ben Rice and AL Cy Young frontrunner Cam Schlittler. The two youngsters from Massachusetts, never highly rated as prospects, have turned themselves into veritable forces at the plate and on the mound, and without their contributions, the injury-riddled 2026 Yankees would almost certainly be spending the final few days of the season playing out the string, not attempting to make a last-ditch run at the AL East while lining up the rotation for a matchup with the Red Sox in the Wild Card round.
MLB Trade Rumors | Darragh McDonald: Yesterday afternoon, the Yankees announced that Oswaldo Cabrera, the popular utilityman who has been with the organization since 2015, had been claimed off waivers by the Cincinnati Reds. He had been designated for assignment earlier in the week, in order to make room on the 40-man roster for Clarke Schmidt.
Playbill | Logan Culwell-Block: Earlier this summer, former Mets infielder José Iglesias made the jump from the ballfield to the stage, joining the Broadway production of Buena Vista Social Club. Now, a Yankee great will be joining him: yesterday, Bernie Williams announced that he will be joining the show’s pit band for a limited run, from October 22nd through November 29th.

Yankees news: Aaron Boone drops huge Cam Schlittler Cy Young prediction appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Aaron Boone was asked a simple question about Cam Schlittler's impact on the Yankees rotation. His answer skipped straight past the premise.
"He's going to win the Cy Young," Boone said during his pregame press conference. "You got an ace at the top that's pitched like that. That's a good place to start. He's been dominant."
"Well, he's gonna win the Cy Young!"
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Aaron Boone on what Cam Schlittler has meant to the Yankees' rotation this season. pic.twitter.com/VzFIYOzdb4
— YES Network (@YESNetwork) September 18, 2026
The manager is not out on a limb. Through 31 starts and 184 2/3 innings this season, Schlittler owns a 1.95 ERA and a 0.90 WHIP, leading the American League in ERA, innings and WHIP while sitting near the top in strikeouts. He has already set a franchise record with 20 starts of one run or fewer, and he became the fourth-youngest Yankee to reach 200 strikeouts in a season. Dylan Cease is the only serious challenger, and his edge is limited to total strikeouts.
Boone traced the rise back further than this year. "I think he's just continued to get better year in and year out," he said. "This is largely in line with who we saw down the stretch when he got called up last year. Obviously had about as dominant a postseason outing as you could against the Red Sox and it's carried that right into this year."
That October showing came in Schlittler's first playoff run, where he posted a 1.26 ERA across 14 1/3 innings after a 2.96 ERA over 73 regular-season frames as a rookie. A seventh-round pick out of Northeastern in 2022, he has climbed faster than anyone in the organization projected.
Boone credited the makeup as much as the arm. "He's got great stuff. Obviously, he's a tremendous competitor," he said. "He's got a real good way about him, ability to make adjustments start to start, not be overwhelmed by a result start to start, and he's put it all together for a full season now at this level."
Schlittler would be New York's second Cy Young winner in four years after Gerrit Cole in 2023, and his 2026 numbers have outpaced Cole's award-winning campaign. The Yankees have already clinched a playoff berth.

The two starting pitchers entered this game trending in opposite directions. Gerrit Cole had just allowed the most home runs (seven) in a two-start span in his career, while Eduardo Rodriguez is in the midst of a career year with a 2.62 ERA. One of those trends remained — Cole giving up another home run on a fastball — but fortunately the other trend was momentarily halted, the Yankees scoring five in the first off E-Rod to give themselves enough of a cushion to weather Cole’s continued home run woes.
Cole settled down after the Carroll dinger to give the Yankees six innings, by which time the offense all but put this game out of reach. They kept the pressure on, scoring a further four runs including solo home runs by Ben Rice and George Lombard Jr., to cruise to a series-opening victory in the desert, 9-2.
Rodriguez came into this game with an ERA above six in the first inning and an ERA right around two for the subsequent innings combined. That made it imperative that the Yankees find a way to do damage before the home team had a chance to come to bat, especially with the rate Cole is giving up the long ball. They did just that with a clear disciplined approach not to expand the zone against E-Rod’s curveball.
Paul Goldschmidt drew a leadoff walk, Cody Bellinger followed with a single, and Heliot Ramos also walked to load the bases with no outs. Rice drew the Yankees’ third walk in the first four batters to plate Goldschmidt and open the scoring, Goldy, Ramos, and Rice all working full counts before taking the free pass. Amed Rosario then fought off a cutter that handcuffed him up and in, muscling it to the opposite field perfectly between center and left fielder to plate Bellinger as the runners went station to station. A wild pitch allowed Ramos to score and Rice and Rosario to move up to second and third. This set up a two-run ground ball single from Lombard that just got by Geraldo Perdomo’s diving attempt to atone for his defensive misplay in the 13th that allowed the Twins to walk off the Yankees on Wednesday.
Rodriguez struck out Volpe to end the inning giving him three strikeouts in the frame, but the damage was done. The 45 pitches he threw were the most he’s thrown in the first inning in his career. 33 of those pitches fell out of the zone, but only eight induced a chase.
It’s a good thing they hung such a crooked number, because Cole immediately gave two of those runs back. He gave up a leadoff single to Perdomo before yanking an 0-1 four-seamer right into Corbin Carroll’s nitro zone, the three-time All-Star obliterating it to right for a two-run bomb to reduce the Yankees’ lead, 5-2. Rice made sure to immediately tilt the momentum back in his team’s favor. After falling behind 0-2, he stayed back on an elevated heater from E-Rod riding it out the other way and over the fence in left-center for a leadoff bomb, his 39th of the year, to give Cole some more of his cushion back, 6-2.
Cole settled down to work a scoreless third and fourth, helped in part by a sharp uptick in slider usage at the expense of some four-seamers as well as an impressive sliding catch in left-center by Spencer Jones in the third. He finally began dialing the fastball command to the corners in the fifth, striking out Tim Tawa and Lars Nootbaar on four-seamers to end the frame after Jesús Sánchez singled with one out. This allowed Lombard to restore the Yankees’ five run lead in the sixth, the rookie punishing a hanging curveball from E-Rod by lining the solo shot down the line it left and into the bullpen for his fourth of the year and third RBI on the night.
The four-seamer was the prime culprit for Cole in his previous two starts with a 68.2-percent hard-hit rate and just six whiffs, and that remained the case tonight. However, I believe it is Cole’s rustiness with his secondaries that is leading his four-seamer to get barreled. The fastball still has plenty of velocity — at 97 mph it’s a full tick above last season. I will grant that he has missed location in the zone on numerous occasions which hasn’t done him any favors.
However, after his last start, Cole identified a lack of chase and whiff against his secondaries as the reason his fastball is getting crushed. Hitters being able to lay off those chase pitches forces Cole to overuse the fastball in counts that favor the softer stuff, which in essence gives them the opportunity to hunt the heater when they should be defending against the breaker. When you can hunt a fastball in any count, chances are you are going to do damage when Cole misses his spot in the zone, the high velocity not much of a weapon when hitters’ bats are preemptively sped up.
Indeed, once he started commanding his slider and knuckle curve to the shadow of the zone in the middle innings, the hard contact against the fastball dried up. Having pitched a strong fifth and sixth and with his pitch count at 90, Boone saw no reason to overextend Cole and ended his night after six with his best innings freshest in mind. He finished night having pitched six innings, allowing two runs on four hits with no walks and six strikeouts.
Despite possessing one of the stingiest bullpens in baseball, the Diamondbacks decided that a five-run deficit in the seventh was too steep to justify using their high leverage arms. So, Zac Gallen made his first career relief appearance, the former All-Star in the midst of am injury-plagued, below-replacement-level campaign. He allowed a leadoff single to Goldschmidt and walked Ramos and Rice — again, both in full counts — to load the bases with one out. Aaron Boone sent out Ryan McMahon to pinch-hit for Rosario, and he hit a sharp grounder to first that Pavin Smith gloved but airmailed the underhand toss to Gallen covering first as all the runners were safe and a run scored on the error. Spencer Jones then appeared to ground into the inning-ending double play, but his hustle out of the box and down the line just beat the throw to pick up an RBI and make it 9-2.
Ryan Yarbrough pitched 1.1 innings in relief of Cole and worked himself into and out of trouble in the seventh. Arizona put runners on second and third as Nolan Arenado singled and Carroll doubled with one out. However, Yarbrough struck out Jose Fernandez and Tawa to strand the pair in scoring position. Rice smoked his fourth triple of the year in the ninth but was stranded at third by a McMahon strikeout. Michael Fulmer and Luis Gil recorded the final five outs of the game without allowing a baserunner to seal the win, 9-2. With the Rays having lost to the Red Sox earlier in the evening, the Yankees’ deficit is back to four games in the division, making that looming four-game set against Tampa in the Bronx even more high stakes.
Cam Schlittler looks to cement his AL Cy Young case tomorrow after Dylan Cease suffered his shortest start of the season on Friday. The Yankees ace will face off against Brandon Pfaadt with a slightly more reasonable game start time. First pitch is scheduled for 8:10 pm ET with the broadcast remaining on YES.
Yankees rout the D-Backs, 9-2, who's your Player of the Game?
Gerrit Cole pitched 6 innings of 2-run ball. George Lombard Jr. hit a two-run single and a solo homer. Ben Rice raked with a solo homer, triple, and two walks.

PHOENIX -- Cam Schlittler sported a significant bruise on his right hamstring as he moved through the visiting clubhouse at Chase Field on Friday afternoon. It was a souvenir from his most recent start, which ended after the Mets’ Bo Bichette connected on a 111.5 mph comebacker.
That ball dented flesh, but Schlittler’s season has been so charmed, even the hard-hit balls are turning into outs. Bichette’s knock ricocheted to catcher Austin Wells, who tossed on to first base, sealing Schlittler’s six scoreless innings that day.
“It’s fun to watch. It’s fun to play behind,” Cody Bellinger said. “Even in the middle of the game, I was like, ‘This is unbelievable.’ You don’t really get that much.”
And while the league has had ample opportunity to take in Schlittler’s dominance, what impresses most from a distance of 60 feet and six inches?
“Probably the composure on the mound,” Wells said. “I think that’s the most impressive, besides obviously the numbers across the board. It’s just the way he handles every inning, every pitch. He expects the best every time he throws the ball. So it’s super impressive.”
That’s good news for the Yankees, who appear to be lining up Schlittler to start a potential Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
“You’ve got an ace at the top that’s pitched like that, that’s a good place to start,” manager Aaron Boone said. “He’s been dominant. I think he’s just continued to get better, year in and year out.”
“The expectation is to make the playoffs, and the expectation is to win a championship,” Schlittler said. “We’re in a good spot if we keep playing the way we’re playing.”
With Schlittler deep into his longest season yet, Wells believes his batterymate is finding new layers of sharpness.
“I think we’ve seen games where he doesn’t have the best command, but he still gets through it,” Wells said. “There’s another layer to that command piece, that makes it effectively a little bit wild sometimes. I think when he continues to improve that, he’s just going to continue to get better.”
Schlittler’s 1.95 ERA is the second-lowest by a Yankee through 31 starts since Ron Guidry’s 1.71 ERA in 1978, when “Louisiana Lightning” won the Cy Young and finished second in the MVP race to Jim Rice of the Red Sox.
It was the 21st time Schlittler has allowed one run or fewer. That’s a franchise record, and over the last 110 years, only three pitchers age 25 or younger have had as many: Blake Snell (2018), Dean Chance (1964) and Babe Ruth (1916).
Yet Boone said he’s not surprised by Schlittler’s performance, saying it has been largely in line with what the Yankees saw after his late-season callup in 2025.
“He had about as dominant a postseason outing as you could against the Red Sox, and he has carried that right into this year,” Boone said. “He’s got great stuff, he’s a tremendous competitor and he has a real good way about him -- an ability to make adjustments start to start, not be overwhelmed by a result start to start, and he’s put it all together for a full season now at this level.”

The New York Yankees could make a surprising move on Anthony Volpe.
Volpe has had success since being recalled, but George Lombard Jr. has taken over as the starting shortstop. So, Volpe's future in New York is very much up in the air.
New York will begin a three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday.
New York Yankees Surprise Anthony Volpe Decision
Although Volpe has been playing better, he isn't guaranteed a spot on the Yankees playoff roster.
After New York clinched a playoff spot, Yankees analysts Bryan Hoch and Patrick Donnelly of MLB.com revealed the likely playoff roster, and they didn't have Volpe on it.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Aaron Judge, Heliot Ramos
DH: Ben Rice
SP: Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole
RP: David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Tim Hill, Ryan Yarbrough, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, Ryan Weathers, Will Warren
The Yankees leaving Volpe off the playoff roster would be a disappointing outcome for the shortstop. It also could signal the end of his tenure in New York as Lombard is the shortstop of the future.
Volpe is hitting .253 with 2 home runs and 26 RBIs this season with the Yankees.
New York Right Now
The Yankees have clinched a playoff spot as New York will be hosting a Wild Card series again.
"Every year you go through a lot, it seems like. But we've been through a lot this year with injuries, with adversity," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "But credit to them for coming together. Through all the ups and downs, they've been a together group. I feel like they've developed a lot of grit over the season."
However, despite clinching a playoff spot, the Yankees made it clear the job isn't finished. New York likely won't win the AL East again, which is frustrating, but the Yankees have confidence they can go on a deep playoff run.
The Yankees are 88-64 and 5 games back of the Tampa Bay Rays for the top spot in the AL East.

History and common sense (we know, two things that don’t always share space in a conversation) typically dictate that a $162 million pitcher doesn’t make a playoff roster for one of two reasons: injuries or disaster.
Luckily for the New York Yankees, that’s not the problem with veteran lefty Carlos Rodón. The three-time All-Star is healthy after multiple elbow problems, and he’s recorded a 2.95 ERA and 1.6 bWAR over 11 starts. Depending on how confident you feel about Gerrit Cole, we’d argue that Rodón is the Yankees’ third-best starter behind AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler and the always-reliable Max Fried.
Yet all signs point to Cole, and not Rodón, starting a potential Game 3 in the Wild Card Series. In fact, some who cover the Yankees have even listed the latter as someone who could be on the roster bubble, at least for the first round.
The New York Yankees must turn to Carlos Rodón rather than Gerrit Cole in the playoffs
We addressed the Cole vs. Rodón debate earlier this week, so we don’t want to make things too repetitive. The bottom line is that Cole has allowed far more home runs at Yankee Stadium than on the road, and the Yankees would host all three games (if needed) in the Wild Card Series. Theoretically, that’d set Rodón up to possibly pitch Game 1 of the ALDS, which would either be against the No. 1 Rays or whoever earns the No. 2 seed; as of Friday afternoon, that honor would go to the AL Central-leading White Sox.
Let’s take a quick look at how Cole and Rodón fare in several key departments:
| Stat | Carlos Rodón | Gerrit Cole |
|---|---|---|
| Batters faced | 315 | 475 |
| Batting average against | .178 | .241 |
| Walk rate | 12.1 percent | 4.2 percent |
| Strikeout rate | 26.3 percent | 24.6 percent |
| Home runs allowed | Seven | 20 |
| Doubles | 12 | 21 |
| Triples | Zero | Two |
| Hit batsmen | 2 | 2 |
The knock against Rodón, though, is his career-worst 12.1 percent walk rate, which is significantly above his lifetime 9.0 average. He hasn't exceeded a 9.0 percent walk rate over a full season since a 10.8 mark in 2018. Assuming that the Yankees don’t overtake the Rays in the AL East, they’d host the Red Sox in the first round.
But here's the good news: The Red Sox have drawn 491 walks, well below the league average of 516. So you’d think that Rodón has the leg up on Cole, right? Interestingly, the Red Sox have only hit 158 home runs, which is tied for seventh-worst in baseball. Much of their offense comes from doubles — their 272 two-baggers are one off the Royals for the MLB lead — and the occasional bruise; the Red Sox’s 93 hit-by-pitches are tied with the Angels for the league lead.
Call us boring, but we’d much rather have the guy who works around walks instead of the 36-year-old with a penchant for giving up home runs. Naturally, that means we should prepare for Cole to throw seven shutout innings during his first playoff start, but what do we know?

If there's one reason to think the New York Yankees have a minuscule chance of overcoming a five-game deficit in the American League East, it's the probable pitchers every series. Aaron Boone's Bombers can feature one of his many frontline starters on a given night, and in this series against the Arizona Diamondbacks, two of his four best pitchers take the mound.
On paper, you see the first two starters and think the advantage should go to the Yankees, but one issue in particular has hampered their former Cy Young winner. If this team is going to make any noise in the postseason, he'll have to work on it, and it starts with this series.
Friday, Sept. 18 (9:40 p.m. ET): Gerrit Cole (NYY) vs. Eduardo Rodriguez (ARI)
Eduardo Rodriguez has proven to be a playoff-caliber pitcher, and his 2.62 ERA in 178.1 IP is frontline stuff. He is the type of high-level arm they'll see in the postseason. Rodriguez typically pitches to contact, holding opposing batters to an 87.3 MPH average exit velocity and a 33% hard-hit rate. This can be one of those games where the Yankees hit ground balls against him for 7+ innings.
Cole, meanwhile, has been snakebit by the long ball, and it isn't so wild to say that the advantage could go to Rodriguez in this one if Cole pitches the way he has. It's been a concerning turn of events ever since that game against the San Diego Padres. For now, the advantage goes to Rodriguez, who'll want to harken back to his Boston days and shut down the Yankees.
Saturday, Sept. 19 (8:10 p.m. ET): Cam Schlittler (NYY) vs. Brandon Pfadt (ARI)
Pfaadt, though, isn't a slouch by any means, and if the Yankees are going to be without Aaron Judge — which usually means the offense will be listless — what can be said about Rodriguez applies to Pfaadt here.
The 27-year-old Arizona starter has a 68th-percentile groundball rate and holds hitters to a 35.5% hard-hit rate. It could be another instance of the Yankees hitting a ton of ground balls. Most competent offenses should be able to hold their own, but it's hard to trust the Yankees 1-through-9 these days. They might need a great pitching performance by Schlittler and win one of those 2-0 or 3-0 games here.
Pfaadt has one of the best walk rates in baseball. His 5.7% BB% is in the 91st percentile, so he'll force them to make contact, and that can be a recipe for disaster for a team that can't put together runs.
Sunday, Sept. 20 (4:10 p.m. ET): Will Warren (NYY) vs. Corbin Burnes (ARI)
Corbin Burnes has pitched all of 7.2 innings this season. He's coming back from Tommy John surgery, which he had last June. It feels like a quick recovery, and he'll likely be on a pitch limit. That said, the sooner the Yankees can get him back in the game, the better.
Every Warren start can't be a high-scoring affair because he can be brilliant or a disaster, so hopefully they get a brilliant Warren here while also chasing Burnes out of the game quickly. If he's out by the third, they can ground down that bullpen.
Warren is coming off a solid outing against the Twins earlier this week, where he allowed five hits, two runs (zero earned), two walks, and racked up six strikeouts in 5.2 innings.
The advantage should go to the Yankees if Warren gives them length, but again, as with any game, it will come down to whether they can score.

item.content:encoded:
The two most valuable Yankees this season are a starting pitcher named Cam Schlittler, from Walpole, Mass., and Northeastern University, a school within walking distance of Fenway Park, and Ben Rice, who comes out of Cohasset, Mass., on the state’s South Shore, about 30 miles from Fenway. If the Yankees are hosting a Wild Card Series against the Red Sox in less than two weeks -- at Yankee Stadium and not Fenway -- Schlittler and Rice will be the biggest reasons.
Schlittler ought to win the AL Cy Young Award and ought to be an MVP candidate for the whole league. David Cone, now a Yankees broadcaster for the YES network and once a great Yankee himself, has one word to describe what he’s seen from Schlittler this season:
“Nails.”
Here’s a breakdown of Schlittler’s ERA, month by month after one start in March, when, of course, he threw a shutout (eight strikeouts) into the sixth inning against the Giants:
1.73 in April
1.48 in May
3.38 in June
1.93 in July
2.33 in August
0.86 so far in September
Carlos Rodón got hurt. Max Fried got hurt. Gerrit Cole joined the season late, and he hasn’t looked like his own Cy Young self lately. It is been Schlittler who has been the Yankees' ace, who is their Game 1 guy, who has carried the staff. He is not going to end up with a 25-3 record and an ERA of 1.74 the way Ron Guidry did nearly 50 years ago. But Schlittler is at 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA going into his last few starts of the regular season. He has been the first young power starter out of the Yankees’ system since Guidry to be this good, and this dominant.
But Rice has been just as important to their offense.
In a season when Aaron Judge was gone for more than 80 games because of a fracture to his rib cage. Then, after Judge finally got back into the lineup and even hit his first home run in months, he left a game against the Twins the other day because of pain in his lower leg. It is why you have to believe, if and when Judge is back in the lineup again, he’s going to be a swing and a prayer the rest of the way.
So No. 99 went away. So did Cody Bellinger, the Yankees’ second-most important hitter a year ago, before he finally returned from the IL. But even when the Yankees struggled to score runs, and even in a roller-coaster year that saw Rice hit just .196 in June and .184 in August, it is Rice who has been the Yankees' hitting star, coming into a weekend series against the Diamondbacks with 38 home runs and still with a chance to knock in 100.
Luis García Jr. showed up from the Nationals at the Trade Deadline to give him some backup. Bellinger has been on a heater since coming off the IL, with five homers, 18 RBIs and a .344 average over his last 22 games. But it was Rice around whom the Yankees built what offense they had before all that, while they were staying ahead of the Red Sox and at least maintaining contact with the Rays.
You know how many homegrown Yankees have hit 40 or more home runs in a season in the last 75 years? Two. One was named Mickey Mantle and the other is Judge. There have been other Yankees sluggers who got to 40 and beyond. Alex Rodriguez once made it all the way to 57. But they all came from somewhere else. Rice is the same as Schlittler: He hasn’t just come to this moment from New England, he’s someone the Yankees drafted in the 12th round of the 2021 Draft (Schlittler was out of the seventh round the following year).
Alfonso Soriano made his own run at 40 more than 20 years ago. Did it twice. But Soriano came to the Yankees as a free agent from Japan. So think about the company Rice will be keeping if does get to 40 homers, starting with his chance this weekend against the Diamondbacks:
Mantle. Judge.
Here is something Rice’s manager, Aaron Boone, has said about him:
"I got my first taste of him in Spring Training of '24, and it was like, 'Oh, OK.' But then this year, it's gone to even another level.”
Here is something else:
“I think he's turning into one of the best hitters in the league."
Rice himself has predictably low-keyed what he’s done for the Yankees so far.
"The year is still in progress, you know?” he said. “It's still going on. We've got more games to play and a long road ahead, so I can't really look back and assess it fully yet."
It really has been a roller-coaster ride occasionally. He has struggled occasionally against left-handed pitchers, but his season-long average against them stands at .254 with 10 home runs and 29 RBIs.
We know what Schlittler’s numbers are. Rice’s, though, can get a little lost sometimes. But in a year where he’s batted everywhere from leadoff to cleanup, when Judge was gone for more than half the time, he has been indispensable, too. And still has a shot to be a 40-homer guy for the Yankees.

Some New York Yankees fans had been wondering if the team would start to limit Cam Schlittler’s innings or even potentially skip one of his remaining starts with the playoffs in view, but it doesn’t appear that the Yankees are planning on that. At least for now.
The Yankees have locked in their starting pitchers for this weekend’s three-game series in Arizona, and the headline assignment is Schlittler taking the ball Saturday against the Diamondbacks, via MLB.com.
With the club already in the postseason but still chasing both the American League East title and the top Wild Card seed, every start carries extra weight.
Manager Aaron Boone’s staff listed Gerrit Cole for Friday, Schlittler for Saturday, and Will Warren for Sunday, setting up a rotation that showcases the team’s depth heading into the final stretch.
Schlittler’s outing is the one that stands out. The right-hander has been the anchor of New York’s staff all year, posting a 14-6 record with a 1.95 ERA and 228 strikeouts.
Those numbers have made him the clear favorite for the American League Cy Young Award and, in the view of many around the league, the best pitcher in baseball this season … although he has already racked up 184.2 innings. He will face Arizona’s Brandon Pfaadt, who enters with a 7-3 mark and a 3.77 ERA.
The contrast is sharp: a dominant, high-strikeout ace against a solid but far less overwhelming counterpart.
The Yankees’ pitching staff as a whole has been exceptional. Their 3.19 team ERA ranks first in the majors, and they lead the league in fewest earned runs and runs allowed.
They have done it despite injuries that forced constant adjustments. Schlittler’s consistency has allowed Boone to manage the rest of the rotation with an eye toward October.
After this series, the club expects to have Max Fried and Carlos Rodón lined up for Tuesday’s doubleheader against the Tampa Bay Rays, with Cole and Schlittler available later in that set.
Sunday’s starter, Will Warren, has quietly put together a strong campaign of his own (10-6, 3.89 ERA). How Boone uses him in the postseason—whether as a fifth starter or a high-leverage reliever—will be one of the more interesting decisions of the coming weeks.
For now, the immediate focus is this weekend in the desert. Friday’s matchup pits Cole against Eduardo Rodriguez, Sunday features Warren opposite Corbin Burnes, and Saturday belongs to Schlittler.
The Yankees know the Diamondbacks can be dangerous at home, but they also know they possess one of the strongest rotations in the sport.
Giving the ball to Schlittler on Saturday is both a statement of confidence and a practical move. It also demonstrates that New York is not concerned about his workload.
If he continues to pitch the way he has all season, the Yanks will take another step toward securing home-field advantage and heading into October with its best possible alignment. The series begins Friday night. All eyes will be on Saturday.

NUEVA YORK — La candidatura de Cam Schlittler al título de MVP ha reavivado una pregunta que es más antigua que la analítica, más antigua que la sala de vídeo. Incluso más antigua que la mayoría de los que ahora la debaten.
¿Qué significa realmente el valor? Un antiguo as de los Yankees ha vuelto a sacar a colación este debate esta semana, con un lanzador que casi nadie esperaba que entrara en la discusión.
La mayor parte del mundo del deporte se ha decantado por una división clara. Un trofeo para el mejor lanzador, otro para el mejor bateador. Los aficionados de los Yankees llevan más de una década viendo cómo los votantes se inclinan por esa opción.
¿Podrá Schlittler, de 25 años, romper con la tendencia?
Un experto nacional lo dejó muy claro. Analizó el panorama, dijo que la elección era obvia y señaló a un bateador potente de Houston. Según él, caso cerrado.
Pero alguien de los Yankees no estaba dispuesto a dejarlo zanjado tan fácilmente.
La primera temporada completa de Schlittler le ha valido el mejor promedio de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) de todo el béisbol. David Cone, el exlanzador de los Yankees y actual comentarista, se mostró en desacuerdo con la idea de que el MVP de la Liga Americana sea pan comido. Su argumento no tenía que ver con las cifras, sino con la propia palabra.
Una fuente cercana dice que la elección es obvia
La crítica que recibió Cone vino de Ken Rosenthal, de The Athletic. En un vídeo que se publicó el 14 de septiembre, un día después de que Cam Schlittler lanzara seis entradas sin encajar ninguna carrera contra los Mets, Rosenthal reconoció los méritos del lanzador diestro antes de descartar su caso.
Rosenthal mencionó a Yordan Álvarez, de Houston, y a esa temporada ofensiva que los votantes suelen premiar, lo que contradice directamente el argumento de los Yankees. Álvarez llegaba a esta semana con un promedio de bateo de .310, 38 jonrones, 96 carreras impulsadas y un OPS de 1,016, mientras lucha por la Triple Corona de la Liga Americana.
«Yordan Álvarez, en mi opinión, parece la elección más obvia por lo que ha logrado en ataque», dijo Rosenthal.
Esa es la opinión generalizada. Y es precisamente la que Cone se propuso complicar.
Un grande de los Yankees le da un nuevo enfoque al tema
Cone defendió su postura en un programa del New York Post junto a Joel Sherman y Jon Heyman. En lugar de discutir las estadísticas, volvió a la prueba más antigua que ofrece el premio: la de la sustracción. ¿Qué pierde un equipo sin un jugador?
Cone planteó el ejercicio en general. Preguntó dónde estarían los Royals sin Bobby Witt Jr., dónde estarían los Astros sin Álvarez y dónde estarían los Yankees sin su as. En su opinión, eso situaba a Schlittler al mismo nivel que los bateadores.
«Si este año no contaran con Schlittler en los Yankees, ¿dónde estarían?», preguntó Cone. «Schlittler está entre los mejores. Sin duda, merece que se le tenga muy en cuenta».
Es un argumento de peso, teniendo en cuenta la temporada que han tenido los Yankees. Aaron Judge solo jugó 65 partidos por culpa de una lesión, y Gerrit Cole, Max Fried y Carlos Rodón también se perdieron partidos. En medio de toda esa agitación, Schlittler fue la constante al frente de la rotación, un lanzador titular en su primer año que llevó al equipo a luchar por el título.
El dato que le mantiene en la carrera
Este es el detalle que mantiene vivo el argumento de Cone, y que pocos medios han destacado. Bradford Doolittle, de ESPN, elabora un índice global llamado AXE, y en su análisis de premios de septiembre situó a Schlittler en segundo lugar entre todos los candidatos al MVP de la Liga Americana. Álvarez lideraba la clasificación con 146,9. Schlittler le seguía de cerca con 143,0.
No es una diferencia abismal. Es un empate casi perfecto en un modelo diseñado para combinar el lanzamiento y el bateo en una sola cifra, y mantiene al as de los Yankees en la lucha. Doolittle seguía diciendo que era una tarea difícil.
Las cifras lo explican todo. Doolittle describió una sucesión de acontecimientos casi perfecta. Schlittler probablemente necesitaría al menos una salida más, seguramente una larga en la que no encajara ninguna carrera, para hacerse con el título de mejor promedio de carreras limpias permitidas de las Grandes Ligas en solitario, en lugar de solo liderar la Liga Americana.
Ni siquiera un final impecable bastaría por sí solo. Álvarez también tendría que quedarse sin la Triple Corona mientras los Astros no se clasifican para los playoffs, y Junior Caminero, de Tampa Bay, necesitaría tener una última semana pésima que hiciera perder a los Rays el liderato de la División Este de la Liga Americana. Es una situación casi imposible, y por eso llama tanto la atención que Doolittle esté dispuesto a incluir a Schlittler en su clasificación.
Unas estadísticas que dan que hablar
Las cifras que lo acompañan explican por qué se le menciona. Schlittler tiene un balance de 14-6, con una ERA de 1,95, 228 strikeouts, un WHIP de 0,90 y un bWAR de 7,1 en 31 partidos como titular. Su marca de 1,95 le empata con Jacob Misiorowski, de Milwaukee, en la mejor ERA de la liga.
El contexto de los récords es aún más impresionante. Las 21 salidas de Schlittler en las que solo ha cedido una carrera o ninguna suponen un récord de los Yankees en una sola temporada, según Sarah Langs, de MLB.com. No se trata solo de un mes brillante. Son siete meses de control casi total por parte de un lanzador novato.
Últimamente ha estado aún mejor, con una ERA de 0,86 este mes, mientras supera las 180 entradas. Varios medios lo sitúan como líder de la Liga Americana en WAR de Baseball-Reference, la métrica exacta que mide el valor que describió Cone. Su ERA también se encuentra entre las más bajas de un lanzador titular de los Yankees desde el 1,74 de Ron Guidry en 1978.
Una votación que gira en torno a una definición
La historia pone de relieve lo que está en juego. Justin Verlander, en 2011, fue el último lanzador a tiempo completo en ganar el MVP de la Liga Americana, y Clayton Kershaw, en 2014, fue el último lanzador en ganarlo en cualquiera de las dos ligas. Ningún lanzador a tiempo completo de los Yankees ha conseguido el premio desde Spud Chandler en 1943.
Por eso este tira y afloja va más allá de un solo nombre. Rosenthal valora el rendimiento a través de los resultados. Cone lo valora a través de la ausencia. Ambos puntos de vista son defendibles, y ninguna votación resolverá cuál es el correcto.
Los Yankees, con la mirada puesta en octubre, preferirían que su as reservara lo mejor de sí mismo para la postemporada, independientemente de los trofeos. Pero, con una o dos salidas por delante, Schlittler todavía tiene margen para dar un empujoncito al debate. Por ahora, el tema sigue abierto, y un grande de los Yankees insiste en que la pregunta más antigua de este deporte aún merece una respuesta.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

The Yankees squandered a chance to sweep the Twins Wednesday, dropping a 13-inning gut punch that diminished their chances of catching up to the Rays in the AL East. They’ll head to Phoenix this weekend for a three-game set against the Diamondbacks, who’ve dropped consecutive series and are hanging by a thread in the NL Wild Card race. With a four-game set against the Rays looming next week, this series against Arizona will be crucial in determining if the Yankees control their own destiny heading into the season’s final week. Let’s take a look at the likely starting pitching matchups.
Friday: Gerrit Cole vs. Eduardo Rodriguez (9:40 pm ET)
Tonight at Chase Field, all eyes will be on Gerrit Cole. Aside from the importance of the game on its own merits, it will be a crucial opportunity for the longtime Yankees ace to show whether he can still be counted upon as a frontline starter this postseason. After posting an exemplary 3.11 ERA in his first 16 starts back from Tommy John surgery, he’s stumbled in his last four, allowing 15 runs in 22.2 innings. Most concerning has been his battle with the long ball, having allowed seven in his last two starts. With Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, and Carlos Rodón firing on all cylinders, a strong outing tonight will help reassure the Yankees that Cole’s recent struggles are just a blip and that he belongs squarely in their playoff rotation.
Cole will face a fellow veteran hurler who’s in the midst of a career year. At the age of 33, Eduardo Rodríguez made his first All-Star team this year and has been a rock for the D-Backs, going 15-6 with a 2.62 ERA that quietly ranks fourth in the NL. Opponents are hitting below the Mendoza line against his heater and are slugging just .335 against his changeup, his top complementary pitch. The latter weapon has been particularly effective against righties, against whom the southpaw has fared batter this year than his fellow lefties. Rodríguez labored his last time out, allowing six runs in 5.1 innings, though only three were earned as the D-Backs committed two costly errors in the fifth.
Saturday: Cam Schlittler vs. Brandon Pfaadt (8:10 pm ET)
When the conversation turns from Cy Young to MVP, you’ve entered rarified air. If the season ended today, Cam Schlittler’s 2026 would rank second in Yankees history in WHIP (0.904) and eighth in ERA (1.95). He’s already seventh in strikeouts (228) and could easily crack the top three with two more representative outings. The last time Schlittler allowed more than a run in one of his starts was on August 3rd. He allowed no runs and one hit in his last outing as he ran roughshod over the Mets. At this point in the season, Schlittler is as close to a sure thing as it gets.
He’s lined up to face Brandon Pfaadt. A hero of the D-Backs’ run to the World Series in 2023, Pfaadt has struggled to establish himself in the intervening years. After spending some time in the bullpen and in the minors this year, he rejoined the rotation on June 30 and has been lights out ever since, going 7-2 with a 2.83 ERA over 12 starts. That ERA was as low as 2.38 before his last outing, a six-run implosion in which he allowed 10 hits to the Rangers in 6.1 innings. Pfaadt doesn’t get many strikeouts but also walks few, relying on soft contact generated by his six-pitch mix to work through lineups.
Thursday: Will Warren vs. Corbin Burnes (4:10 pm ET)
Will Warren may have nine lives. In mid-August, it looked like his days in the rotation were numbered with Rodón scheduled to return from injury. Instead, with Fried and Ryan Weathers landing on the shelf, the 27-year-old got a reprieve. He’s made the most of it, going 2-0 with a 1.38 ERA in his last five outings (four starts) while allowing just two home runs. While he’s unlikely to crack the playoff rotation barring injury, Warren has helped reassert himself as a valuable asset in the bullpen this postseason and in the rotation going forward.
The D-Backs are scheduled to hand the ball to Corbin Burnes. After signing a six-year megadeal with Arizona before the 2025 season, he made only 11 starts before missing a year-plus to Tommy John surgery. Burnes has made just two outings since his return and has looked rusty. His last time out, the former Cy Young Award winner allowed five runs in 4.2 innings to the Marlins. He threw just 75 pitches in that start as he continues to ramp up, and it’s unclear if he’ll be permitted to shoulder a full starter’s workload this time out.

Pitching has been a major strength for the New York Yankees this season, particularly starting pitching. But the Yankees have dealt with numerous pitching injuries with Max Fried (two stints on the IL), Carlos Rodón (two stints on the IL), Ryan Weathers (currently on the IL) and Fernando Cruz (currently on the IL) all going down at certain points of the season. Not to mention, Gerrit Cole and Clarke Schmidt missed time this year while recovering from Tommy John surgery, and Rodón didn't make his season debut until May due to offseason surgery.
So it remains to be seen whether the Yankees' pitching staff will be able to hold up for a deep postseason run. And on Wednesday against the Minnesota Twins, Rodón initially gave Yankees fans cause for concern.
Rodón's concerning dip in velocity vs. Twins
Rodón's fastball velocity was down in the low-90s across the first three innings of his most recent start in Minnesota. The left-hander threw some fastballs at 90 mph to begin the game and averaged 92.6 mph on the pitch, as opposed to his season average of 94.4 mph.
Luckily, Rodón was able to crank things up in his final three innings of work, throwing a number of pitches above 95 mph afterwards. This likely made the Yankees and their fans breathe a sigh of relief for the time being. But Rodón's explanation after the game won't give fans much clarity.
Rodón's explanation
According to Gary Phillips of The New York Daily News, Rodón told reporters that he was dealing with tightness at the beginning of his start, but was able to get loose as his outing progressed. Rodón didn't specify where he was feeling tight/whether it was localized or if he was just trying to say he felt a generalized sense that he couldn't break through the way he wanted to.
So while it's good news that Rodón was able to shake it off after the third, the Yankees should still be worried about his overall durability with the postseason around the corner. Rodón is slated to be the Yankees' No. 4 starter in the playoffs behind Cam Schlittler, Cole and Fried. They will have to hope that his tightness doesn't come back in his next start or in the postseason or snowball into something worse.
As aforementioned, Rodón was out until May of this season after undergoing surgery to remove a bone spur from his left elbow last October. He also dealt with a hamstring issue during his rehab. In addition to his initial IL stint, Rodón missed over a month and a half of action from Jun. 28 to Aug. 18 with left elbow inflammation. The 33-year-old has pitched very well in 15 starts this season (2.95 ERA), but this latest blip should have the Yankees questioning whether they can rely on him the rest of the way.

item.content:encoded:
By any objective measure, Cam Schlittler, in his first full season in the majors, is having one of the best seasons any Yankees starter has ever had.
Schlittler, who is expected to start Saturday against the Diamondbacks in Phoenix, is 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA. Those numbers alone, however, don’t tell the full story of Schlittler’s 2026 season, one that has established him as a co-favorite, along with Dylan Cease of the Blue Jays, for the American League Cy Young Award.
After Schlittler threw six scoreless innings Sunday afternoon in a 2-0 victory over the Mets, manager Aaron Boone even made a push for him to be considered for another award.
“He might be the MVP, too,” Boone said. “It’s been awesome. Just an awesome season.”
That, of course, is a long shot at best. Many voters, not to mention players, see the MVP as the sole dominion of position players, just as the Cy Young Award is reserved for pitchers.
“He’s definitely pitching like an MVP,” Aaron Judge said after Sunday's win. “They’ve got a Cy Young Award for a reason — best pitcher in the game. He’s got my vote definitely for the Cy Young.”
Regardless, Schlittler is in the midst of a strong finishing kick to his year, and it is not a stretch to say he has emerged as the favorite with just over a week left in the regular season.
Though Schlittler has the edge over Cease in many of the numbers — traditional as well as what would be considered more “modern” ones — used when it comes to evaluating pitchers for the Cy Young Award, Cease has some of those in his favor as well.
Digging into many of those numbers, all of them as of Wednesday afternoon:
Schlittler is second in the American League in wins with 14 compared to 11 for Cease (11-6), though Cy Young Award voters have put little emphasis on wins in the last decade-plus.
The Mariners' Felix Hernandez, for instance, won the AL Cy Young Award in 2010 after going 13-12 (with an MLB-leading 2.27 ERA, one of many statistics, both old-school and new-school, in which he led). The Mets' Jacob deGrom won the NL award in 2018 after going 10-9 (with an MLB-best 1.70 ERA and dominating pretty much every other statistical category), and the Pirates' Paul Skenes took NL honors last season after going 10-10 (with an MLB-leading 1.97 ERA and widespread statistical dominance elsewhere).
Schlittler leads Cease in ERA, 1.95 to 2.38; walks and hits per innings pitched (WHIP), 0.90 to 1.06; innings, 184 2/3 to 166 1/3, and Wins above Replacement, 7.0 to 6.1, according to baseball-reference.com, and 5.9 to 5.6, according to Fangraphs.com.
Schlittler also holds the edge in ERA+, a statistic measuring the quality of a pitcher’s ERA compared to the league average, adjusting to the ballpark he pitches in, with the league average being 100.
Cease’s ERA+ is 185, a terrific, Cy Young Award-worthy number in many years, but this year it ranks him second in the AL to Schlittler’s extraordinary ERA+ of 216 (deGrom’s ERA+ in 2018 was 218, Skenes’ in 2025 was 226).
Schlittler's “calling card” from the time he was promoted to the big leagues in July 2025 has been command, according to Boone, and he dominates Cease in that category as well.
Despite pitching 18 1/3 more innings, Schlittler has walked only 44 batters to Cease's 72. Schlittler ranks fifth in the AL in walks per nine innings at 2.1 and Cease ranks 22nd at 3.9.
Cease does have some numbers in his favor.
Despite throwing 18 1/3 fewer innings, Cease has 236 strikeouts, tied for the MLB lead, to Schlittler’s 228, giving the former a ratio of 12.8 strikeouts per nine innings to the latter’s 11.1. Cease has 13 games with at least nine strikeouts, the most of any pitcher in the AL, and Schlittler has seven such games.
Cease has been slightly harder to hit, with opposing batters producing a .177 batting average against, which leads the AL among qualified starting pitchers, compared to a .185 batting average against for Schlittler (which ranks him second in that category). Cease is allowing 5.7 hits per nine innings and Schllittler is allowing 6.0.
Cease has allowed only 11 homers in his 166 1/3 innings and Schlittler has allowed 16 in his 184 2/3 innings.
Cease also holds the edge over Schlittler in Fielding Independent Pitching (FIP), which attempts to measure a pitcher’s performance based on those elements he directly controls before a ball is put in play and the vagaries of defense become a factor. Those would be strikeouts, walks, homers allowed and hit batsmen.
Cease leads the AL in FIP at 2.48. Schlittler is second at 2.57.
Though Cease does hold an advantage in some of the difficulty-to-hit categories, they likely won’t be enough — at the moment, anyway — to deny Schlittler's bid to become the seventh Yankee to win a Cy Young Award (Gerrit Cole was the most recent in 2023).
And there’s this: Schlittler’s closing argument has been especially eye-popping. He’s allowed one run or fewer in an MLB-leading (and franchise-record) 21 starts this season, including in each of his last seven starts, going 4-0 with a 1.00 ERA and a 0.76 WHIP in that span. He has a 0.81 ERA and 0.72 WHIP in those 21 games. In two other games, he allowed zero or one earned run.
Schlittler has allowed three or fewer runs in 27 of his 31 starts and two or fewer in 24 of them.
Cease has 16 outings in which he allowed one run or fewer, certainly an impressive number, but has not pitched quite as well of late, 4-0 with a 2.70 ERA in his previous seven outings.

PHOENIX — There always was the understanding that there would be some bumps along the road in Gerrit Cole’s first season back from Tommy John surgery, as there are with any pitcher returning from major elbow surgery. Yet, for most of his first 20 starts back, he looked like the Cole of old.
The last two, however, have started to ring some moderate alarm bells at an inopportune time — or, if viewed through the Yankees’ pinstriped glasses, a decent time so that he can get himself straightened out over his final two starts before the playoffs.
